characters.name: Ghost of King Hamlet

characters.description: The new king of Denmark and Hamlet's uncle. He has married the widowed Queen Gertrude soon after his brother's death and presents the union as a practical way to steady the country while managing a threat from Norway.
characters.name: Claudius

characters.description: The queen of Denmark, Hamlet's mother, and now Claudius's wife. She wants Hamlet to set aside prolonged mourning and remain at court, apparently hoping the new royal household can restore stability.
characters.name: Gertrude

characters.description: Hamlet's trusted friend from university. Level-headed and cautious about supernatural claims, he nevertheless accepts the evidence of his own eyes and brings news of the apparition to Hamlet.
characters.name: Horatio

characters.description: The king's senior adviser and father of Laertes and Ophelia. He is talkative, confident in his worldly judgment, and strongly inclined to supervise his children's choices.
characters.name: Polonius

characters.description: Polonius's daughter, who has received Hamlet's romantic attention. She is affectionate toward her brother Laertes but constrained by the warnings and commands of the men in her family.
characters.name: Ophelia

characters.description: Polonius's son and Ophelia's brother, preparing to return to France. Protective of Ophelia and confident in courtly conventions, he cautions her against trusting Hamlet's declarations of love.
characters.name: Laertes

characters.description: A childhood acquaintance of Hamlet summoned to Elsinore with Guildenstern. The king and queen ask him to spend time with the prince and discover the cause of his altered behavior.
characters.name: Rosencrantz

characters.description: A childhood acquaintance of Hamlet summoned alongside Rosencrantz. He accepts the royal couple's request to observe Hamlet and report what may be troubling him.
characters.name: Guildenstern

characters.description: A Norwegian prince whose attempt to recover disputed lands concerns the Danish court. Though initially known through reports rather than direct contact, his disciplined military purpose contrasts with the uncertainty inside Elsinore.
characters.name: Fortinbras

characters.description: A cemetery worker preparing Ophelia's grave. He treats death as familiar labor and matches Hamlet's questions with literal answers, riddles, and practical observations about the dead.
characters.name: Gravedigger

recaps.ending: At the arranged fencing match, Hamlet scores the first touches against Laertes but refuses the poisoned wine Claudius has prepared. Gertrude drinks from the cup without knowing the danger and collapses. Laertes then wounds Hamlet with the poisoned blade; in the struggle they exchange weapons, and Hamlet wounds Laertes with it. The dying Laertes admits the plot and identifies Claudius as its author. Hamlet stabs the king and forces him to drink the remaining poison, killing him. Hamlet and Laertes forgive one another before Laertes dies. With the poison overcoming him, Hamlet asks Horatio to live and give an accurate account of the events, then gives his support to Fortinbras as the next ruler and dies. Fortinbras arrives after returning from Poland, finds the Danish royal family destroyed, claims his right to the kingdom, and orders military honors for Hamlet. Horatio remains to explain how revenge, surveillance, accident, and planned murder brought the court to this end.
recaps.in_short: Prince Hamlet returns to Elsinore after his father's death and learns from the dead king's ghost that his uncle Claudius committed the murder before taking the crown and marrying Queen Gertrude. Hamlet adopts an erratic manner while testing the accusation, and a performance recreating the crime convinces him of Claudius's guilt. His delay and secrecy damage Ophelia and draw her father Polonius, her brother Laertes, and Hamlet's former friends into the conflict. Hamlet accidentally kills Polonius and is sent toward execution in England, but escapes. Ophelia loses her reason and drowns; Laertes returns seeking revenge and joins Claudius in a poisoned fencing plot. During the match Gertrude drinks poisoned wine, Laertes and Hamlet are both cut by the poisoned blade, and Laertes exposes the scheme. Hamlet kills Claudius before dying. Horatio survives to tell the story, while Fortinbras enters the ruined court and takes control of Denmark.

recaps.text: On the battlements at Elsinore, guards and Hamlet's friend Horatio see an armed apparition resembling the recently dead King Hamlet. Denmark is also preparing against possible action by the Norwegian prince Fortinbras. Inside the court, the dead king's brother Claudius has taken the throne and married Queen Gertrude. Prince Hamlet remains in mourning and resents both the marriage and the pressure to accept it. Horatio tells him about the apparition. Meanwhile, Laertes prepares to return to France and warns his sister Ophelia that Hamlet's romantic interest may not survive the obligations of royalty. Their father Polonius orders Ophelia to reject Hamlet's approaches. Hamlet goes to the night watch, where the apparition signals that it wants to speak with him alone.

The ghost claims to be Hamlet's father and says Claudius murdered him by pouring poison into his ear. It demands revenge against Claudius but tells Hamlet not to harm Gertrude. Hamlet makes Horatio and the guard Marcellus swear secrecy and hints that he may behave strangely as part of his response. Later, Ophelia reports that Hamlet has visited her in a disturbed state, and Polonius decides frustrated love explains the prince's conduct. Claudius and Gertrude summon Hamlet's old acquaintances Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to learn what is wrong. Hamlet quickly realizes they are acting for the king. A traveling acting company arrives, giving Hamlet a way to test the ghost's accusation: he plans a performance that resembles the alleged murder and will study Claudius's reaction.

Claudius and Polonius secretly observe an encounter between Hamlet and Ophelia. Hamlet rejects her and directs bitter attacks at love, marriage, and deception; Claudius concludes that love alone does not explain his behavior. Hamlet then stages the actors' account of a ruler killed through poison by a relative who wins the widow. Claudius abruptly stops the performance, which Hamlet and Horatio take as confirmation of guilt. Claudius tries to pray, acknowledging his crime to himself but finding that he cannot surrender the benefits gained from it. Hamlet comes upon him and could strike, yet delays because he fears killing a man at prayer may reward rather than punish him. Hamlet instead goes to confront Gertrude in her room while Polonius hides behind a hanging to listen.

During the confrontation with his mother, Hamlet hears movement behind the hanging and thrusts his sword through it, killing Polonius without first seeing whom he has struck. He condemns Gertrude's marriage and sees the ghost again, though Gertrude cannot see it. Claudius now regards Hamlet as immediately dangerous. He sends the prince to England with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, secretly enclosing orders for Hamlet's execution. Hamlet conceals Polonius's body before being forced to reveal its location. On the road he encounters troops connected with Fortinbras and is struck by the contrast between their readiness for action and his own delays. Back at Elsinore, Ophelia is overcome by her father's death and Hamlet's absence, speaking and singing in disordered fragments. Laertes returns at the head of an angry crowd, demanding an account of his father's death.

Hamlet sends word that he has returned to Denmark after pirates intercepted his voyage. Claudius redirects Laertes's anger toward Hamlet and proposes a fencing match in which Laertes will use a sharpened blade coated with poison. Claudius prepares poisoned wine as a second means of ensuring Hamlet's death. Gertrude then reports that Ophelia has drowned after falling into a stream. At the cemetery, Hamlet speaks with a gravedigger and reflects on the remains of people once known to him. The funeral party arrives, and Hamlet realizes the grave is Ophelia's. Laertes leaps into it in grief; Hamlet reveals himself, insists that his love for Ophelia was profound, and struggles with Laertes before they are separated. The court moves toward the fencing match under the appearance of reconciliation.

Hamlet tells Horatio that he discovered the execution order aboard the ship and replaced it with one condemning Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Despite an uneasy feeling, he accepts the fencing match with Laertes. Hamlet apologizes for his earlier conduct, and Laertes outwardly accepts while retaining the poisoned weapon. During the bout Gertrude drinks from Claudius's poisoned cup. Laertes wounds Hamlet; in the ensuing scuffle the men exchange swords, and Hamlet wounds Laertes with the same poisoned point. Gertrude dies, and Laertes confesses the plot and names Claudius. Hamlet kills Claudius with the blade and poisoned drink. Laertes and Hamlet die soon afterward, reconciled. Hamlet charges Horatio to tell the truth and supports Fortinbras's claim before his death. Fortinbras arrives to find the royal house destroyed, assumes authority in Denmark, and orders honors for Hamlet as Horatio prepares to recount the causes of the disaster.

characters.description: A victorious Roman general whose defeat of Pompey's sons has made him the dominant public figure in Rome. Admired by crowds and offered royal honors, he presents confidence and authority while privately showing physical vulnerability and concern about possible threats.
characters.name: Julius Caesar

characters.description: A respected Roman senator and friend of Caesar, known for honor and self-command. Cassius appeals to his concern for the republic, asking him to consider whether Caesar's growing power is compatible with Roman liberty.
characters.name: Marcus Brutus

characters.description: A Roman senator who fears Caesar intends to dominate the republic. Perceptive, resentful, and skilled at persuasion, he begins drawing Brutus toward organized resistance by appealing to Brutus's ancestry and public reputation.
characters.name: Caius Cassius

characters.description: Caesar's loyal friend and an athletic, popular Roman. He offers Caesar a crown during the public celebrations and remains close to him, while Cassius distrusts the strength of that loyalty.
characters.name: Mark Antony

characters.description: A blunt Roman senator who reports that Caesar refused a ceremonial crown three times before collapsing in public. Though initially wary of Cassius's probing, he is troubled by the strange events surrounding Rome and Caesar's rise.
characters.name: Casca

characters.description: Caesar's wife. She is uneasy about danger to her husband and concerned by the warning he receives during the public festival, but Caesar dismisses her immediate fears.
characters.name: Calpurnia

characters.description: A prophetic stranger who publicly warns Caesar to be cautious on the fifteenth of March. Caesar disregards the message, while Brutus and Cassius notice the interruption.
characters.name: Soothsayer

characters.description: A Roman recruited into Cassius's conspiracy against Caesar. He carries forged messages intended to convince Brutus that ordinary citizens expect him to oppose Caesar's ambition.
characters.name: Cinna

characters.description: A young servant in Brutus's household. Loyal and frequently summoned during Brutus's sleepless night, he conveys messages and provides quiet assistance without knowing the full purpose of the secret meeting.
characters.name: Lucius

characters.description: Brutus's wife and the daughter of the republican statesman Cato. She recognizes that Brutus is hiding a serious burden and insists that their marriage entitles her to share his confidence, demonstrating her resolve by enduring a self-inflicted wound.
characters.name: Portia

characters.description: One of the senators conspiring against Caesar. He claims he can overcome Caesar's reluctance to attend the Senate and is assigned to ensure that Caesar comes to the Capitol.
characters.name: Decius Brutus

characters.description: A teacher who has learned the names and intentions of Caesar's enemies. He prepares a written warning listing the conspirators and waits along Caesar's route to the Capitol, hoping Caesar will read it in time.
characters.name: Artemidorus

characters.description: Caesar's adopted heir, summoned toward Rome after the assassination. He joins Antony and Lepidus in a new ruling alliance and takes part in deciding how to defeat Brutus and Cassius.
characters.name: Octavius Caesar

characters.description: A Roman leader allied with Antony and Octavius after Caesar's death. The three include him in their governing coalition and in their severe plans against political enemies, though Antony privately considers him less capable than the others.
characters.name: Lepidus

characters.description: A loyal officer and friend of Cassius in the republican army. He carries messages around the camp as Brutus and Cassius reconcile their commands and prepare to face the triumvirs' forces.
characters.name: Titinius

recaps.ending: At Philippi, Cassius wrongly concludes that Titinius has been captured and has his servant Pindarus help him die with the sword used against Caesar. Titinius returns safely, finds Cassius dead, and kills himself. Brutus's forces continue fighting, but defeat becomes inevitable. Brutus asks several companions to help him die; they refuse until Strato agrees to hold a sword while Brutus runs onto it. Octavius and Antony find the body. Antony distinguishes Brutus from the other conspirators, judging that he acted from a sincere, though mistaken, concern for Rome rather than envy. Octavius orders an honorable burial and absorbs Brutus's surviving followers into the victorious side. Caesar's murder has therefore failed to preserve the republic: the conspirators are dead, their armies defeated, and power belongs to the triumvirs led by Caesar's heir and Antony.
recaps.in_short: As Julius Caesar returns to Rome in triumph, Cassius fears that he will become a monarch and recruits respected senator Brutus into a conspiracy. Brutus agrees because he believes Caesar's potential ambition threatens the republic. Despite omens and warnings, Caesar goes to the Senate, where the conspirators stab him. Brutus permits Caesar's ally Mark Antony to speak at the funeral. Antony uses Caesar's wounds and will to turn the crowd against the assassins, forcing Brutus and Cassius from Rome. Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus form a triumvirate and wage war on them. Brutus and Cassius quarrel but reconcile before meeting the opposing army at Philippi. After military reversals and mistaken reports, Cassius and his loyal officer Titinius kill themselves. Brutus, facing defeat, also dies by suicide. Antony honors Brutus's public motive, but the conspirators' attempt to save republican liberty ends with Caesar's heirs victorious.

recaps.text: Julius Caesar returns to Rome after defeating Pompey's sons, and the public celebrates him. Tribunes object that the crowd has transferred its loyalty too quickly from Pompey. During the festival of Lupercal, a soothsayer warns Caesar about the fifteenth of March, but Caesar dismisses him. Cassius begins sounding out Brutus, a senator admired for honor, about Caesar's growing power. Brutus loves Caesar personally but admits concern for Rome. Casca reports that Mark Antony publicly offered Caesar a crown three times and that Caesar refused it each time before collapsing. Caesar privately identifies Cassius as dangerous. That night, unnatural storms and ominous sights disturb Rome. Cassius interprets them as signs against Caesar and recruits Casca. He sends Cinna to place forged appeals where Brutus will find them, making resistance appear to be a public demand.

Unable to sleep, Brutus decides that Caesar must die, not for proven abuses but because kingship might transform him into a tyrant. The forged messages reinforce that conclusion. Cassius and the conspirators visit, and Brutus takes command of key decisions: they will not swear an oath, will exclude Cicero, and will kill only Caesar rather than Antony as well. Portia presses Brutus to explain his distress, proving her constancy, but their conversation is interrupted. On the morning of the Senate meeting, Calpurnia's nightmare and alarming reports from priests persuade Caesar to remain home. Decius reinterprets the dream as a sign of Rome drawing strength from Caesar and suggests the Senate may mock him or withdraw a crown. Caesar changes his mind. Artemidorus prepares a warning that names the conspirators, and Portia anxiously sends Lucius toward the Capitol.

On the way to the Capitol, Caesar again dismisses the soothsayer and fails to read Artemidorus's warning. At the Senate, the conspirators surround him under cover of a petition and stab him; Brutus's participation completes Caesar's shock and collapse. Mark Antony sends assurances, then returns and outwardly reconciles with the assassins while privately grieving over Caesar's body. Brutus rejects Cassius's caution and allows Antony to speak at the funeral after Brutus explains the killing. Brutus tells the citizens that he acted to prevent slavery under an ambitious ruler, and the crowd initially approves. Antony then reminds them of Caesar's generosity, displays the wounds, and reveals a will benefiting Roman citizens. The crowd turns violently against the conspirators, who flee the city, while Antony recognizes that he has released forces he may not control.

The enraged mob kills an innocent poet named Cinna merely because he shares a conspirator's name. Antony, Octavius, and Lepidus form a triumvirate, draw up lists of people to be executed, and prepare to fight Brutus and Cassius. At the republican camp, Brutus accuses Cassius of tolerating corruption; their quarrel becomes intensely personal before they reconcile. Brutus then reveals that Portia has died by suicide after becoming overwhelmed by his absence and the triumvirs' strength. Despite Cassius's strategic preference to wait, Brutus decides their army should march to Philippi. That night, Caesar's ghost appears to Brutus and says they will meet again there. Brutus continues toward battle, carrying both private grief and the consequences of his public choice.

The rival leaders confront one another at Philippi before battle. Brutus and Cassius recognize that capture would mean humiliation and agree they will not be led through Rome as prisoners. Brutus's troops gain an advantage over Octavius but begin plundering too soon, while Antony's forces overwhelm Cassius's position. From a hill, Cassius asks Pindarus to report what is happening to Titinius. Pindarus mistakenly believes the approaching troops have captured Titinius, so Cassius concludes that all is lost and orders Pindarus to help him die with the same sword that struck Caesar. Titinius was actually welcomed by allied soldiers. When he returns and finds Cassius dead because of the error, he kills himself with Cassius's sword. Brutus arrives, mourns both men, and prepares for another engagement.

The second phase of battle destroys the remaining republican resistance. Young Cato dies fighting, while Lucilius pretends to be Brutus so that enemy soldiers will capture him and give the real Brutus time to escape. Antony recognizes the deception and treats Lucilius with respect. With defeat certain, Brutus asks his companions to help him die rather than be captured. Several refuse, but Strato finally holds a sword while Brutus runs onto it. Octavius and Antony then reach the body. Antony declares that Brutus alone among the conspirators acted from an honest belief that Caesar's death served Rome, whereas the others were driven by envy. Octavius orders an honorable burial and accepts Brutus's surviving men into his service. The triumvirs leave the battlefield victorious, and the republican conspiracy ends in military and political failure.

characters.description: The aging king of Britain, preparing to divide his realm among his three daughters while retaining the name and ceremonial privileges of kingship. He makes each daughter's inheritance depend on a public declaration of love.
characters.name: Lear

characters.description: Lear's eldest daughter and Albany's wife. She answers her father's public test with extravagant praise and receives a large share of Britain.
characters.name: Goneril

characters.description: Lear's second daughter and Cornwall's wife. She echoes Goneril's declarations during the division of the kingdom and is rewarded with an equally rich portion.
characters.name: Regan

characters.description: Lear's youngest daughter, sought in marriage by Burgundy and the King of France. She refuses to turn genuine affection into exaggerated public flattery, provoking Lear to disown her.
characters.name: Cordelia

characters.description: A loyal nobleman who challenges Lear's treatment of Cordelia and is banished for speaking plainly. His devotion to the king survives the sentence.
characters.name: Kent

characters.description: A senior nobleman at Lear's court and father of Edgar and Edmund. He acknowledges Edmund as his son while noting the social difference created by Edmund's birth outside marriage.
characters.name: Gloucester

characters.description: Gloucester's younger son, recently returned to court after years away. Resentful that the law favors his legitimate brother Edgar, he privately resolves to win the status and inheritance denied by his birth.
characters.name: Edmund

characters.description: Goneril's husband and one of Lear's sons-in-law, awarded control of half the kingdom through the division. He is less forceful than his wife at the opening court ceremony.
characters.name: Albany

characters.description: Regan's husband and Albany's fellow ruler after Lear divides Britain. He receives power over the other half of the kingdom.
characters.name: Cornwall

characters.description: Cordelia's royal suitor. After Lear withdraws her inheritance, he values her honesty and character above a dowry and takes her as his queen.
characters.name: France

characters.description: One of Cordelia's suitors. When Lear strips away her wealth and title, Burgundy declines to marry her without the promised inheritance.
characters.name: Burgundy

characters.description: Gloucester's legitimate elder son and legal heir. Trusting his younger brother Edmund, he is bewildered when Edmund warns that their father has suddenly turned against him.
characters.name: Edgar

characters.description: Goneril's steward and an efficient servant of her household. He follows her order to treat Lear and the king's unruly followers with less deference.
characters.name: Oswald

characters.description: Lear's licensed jester and one of the few companions willing to criticize him openly. Through songs, riddles, and jokes, he points out the danger of surrendering power while expecting to keep its privileges.
characters.name: Fool

recaps.ending: Lear and Cordelia are captured after the French-backed army loses. Edmund secretly orders both killed. Goneril poisons Regan because they are rivals for Edmund, then kills herself when Albany exposes her conspiracy. Edgar defeats Edmund in a formal challenge and reveals his identity; the wounded Edmund admits his crimes and tries too late to stop the executions. Cordelia has already been hanged. Lear enters carrying her body and dies in grief. Gloucester has also died after learning that the disguised son who protected him was Edgar, while Cornwall died earlier from a wound received during Gloucester's blinding. Albany yields authority to Kent and Edgar, but Kent indicates that he will soon follow Lear in death. Edgar is left to bear responsibility for the damaged kingdom.
recaps.in_short: King Lear divides Britain between Goneril and Regan after disowning Cordelia for refusing to flatter him. Once empowered, the elder daughters strip away his followers and authority, driving him into a storm. Meanwhile Edmund frames Edgar, betrays their father Gloucester, and rises by serving Lear's daughters. Cornwall and Regan blind Gloucester, but disguised Edgar guides and protects him. Cordelia returns with French forces to rescue Lear, and the two reconcile. Their army loses; Edmund orders them executed while Goneril and Regan compete for him. Goneril poisons Regan and then kills herself. Edgar defeats Edmund and exposes his treachery, but the reversal comes too late: Cordelia is hanged, and Lear dies holding her body. Albany relinquishes power, Kent expects death, and Edgar is left to govern the ruined realm.

recaps.text: Lear announces that he will divide Britain among his daughters according to how fully they declare their love for him. Goneril and Regan offer elaborate praise; Cordelia refuses to exaggerate. Lear disowns Cordelia, banishes Kent for defending her, and gives power to the two elder daughters and their husbands. France marries Cordelia without a dowry. Edmund, Gloucester's younger son, forges a letter suggesting that Edgar plans to displace their father, then persuades Edgar to flee. At Goneril's home, Lear's large retinue causes conflict. Goneril demands that he reduce it, and Lear curses her before leaving for Regan. Kent returns in disguise to serve Lear, while the Fool repeatedly warns that the king surrendered the power that once protected him.

Edmund stages a fight with Edgar and wounds himself, convincing Gloucester that Edgar is dangerous. Edgar hides by adopting the identity of a destitute wanderer called Poor Tom. Cornwall and Regan punish Kent for quarreling with Oswald, placing him in the stocks despite his service to Lear. When Lear arrives, Regan supports Goneril rather than her father. The sisters reduce the number of followers they will allow him to keep until they question why he needs any. Refusing to submit, Lear rushes out into a violent storm with the Fool; Kent follows to find and protect him. Gloucester privately decides to aid the king despite Cornwall's orders, while Edmund prepares to use that decision against his father.

Exposed to the storm, Lear rages against the weather and begins recognizing the suffering of people who lack shelter and power. Kent leads him to a hut, where they meet Edgar disguised as Poor Tom; Lear, the Fool, and the disguised Edgar form a strange company. Gloucester finds them and arranges help. Edmund shows Cornwall a letter proving Gloucester's assistance to Lear and is rewarded with his father's title. Cornwall and Regan seize Gloucester, blind him, and cast him out. A servant who tries to stop the cruelty wounds Cornwall before Regan kills the servant; Cornwall later dies from the injury. The blinded Gloucester learns that Edgar was falsely accused. Still concealed, Edgar takes charge of his despairing father and guides him toward Dover, where Cordelia's supporters are gathering.

In Dover, Cordelia searches for Lear and brings him under medical care. Gloucester asks his unknown guide to lead him to a cliff so he can end his life. Edgar instead stages a harmless fall on level ground and persuades him that he miraculously survived, restoring some will to continue. Lear, wandering and mentally disordered, meets Gloucester before Cordelia's attendants find him. Lear wakes in Cordelia's care, recognizes her, and asks forgiveness; she answers with compassion. Political conflict grows among the British leaders: Goneril and Regan both desire Edmund, while Albany condemns Goneril and the cruelty done to Gloucester. Edgar kills Oswald and finds Goneril's letter proposing Albany's murder. The French-backed force led by Cordelia prepares to fight the British army commanded by Edmund.

The British army wins, and Lear and Cordelia are captured. Edmund sends them away with a secret order for their deaths. Albany arrests Edmund and Goneril for treason. A disguised Edgar challenges Edmund, defeats him, and identifies himself; he reports that Gloucester died after learning the truth about his loyal son. Regan, poisoned by the jealous Goneril, dies, and Goneril kills herself after her conspiracy is exposed. The dying Edmund admits that he ordered Lear and Cordelia killed and tries to cancel the command, but help arrives too late. Lear carries in Cordelia's body: she has been hanged. Unable to revive her, he dies beside her. Albany offers rule to Kent and Edgar. Kent says his own life is nearly over, leaving Edgar to face the work of governing after the collapse of Lear's family and court.

characters.description: A Scottish nobleman and celebrated soldier serving King Duncan. Courageous in battle and newly honored for defeating rebels, he becomes unsettled when supernatural figures predict a greater title and the crown.
characters.name: Macbeth

characters.description: Macbeth's wife and closest confidante. On reading his account of the prophecy, she immediately considers how the promised crown might be obtained and worries that his scruples could obstruct his ambition.
characters.name: Lady Macbeth

characters.description: Three supernatural figures who meet amid thunder and plan an encounter with Macbeth. Their compressed, paradoxical speech associates them with confusion and moral disorder before their purpose becomes clear.
characters.name: Three Witches

characters.description: A Scottish nobleman and fellow commander who fights alongside Macbeth. Observant and cautious, he hears predictions concerning his descendants but questions whether apparent truths may conceal danger.
characters.name: Banquo

characters.description: The king of Scotland, generous toward loyal service and relieved by victory over rebellion. He rewards Macbeth with a new title and places great trust in the nobleman whose castle he visits.
characters.name: King Duncan

characters.description: Duncan's eldest son and named heir. He supports his father at court and represents the established royal succession that stands between Macbeth and the witches' promise.
characters.name: Malcolm

characters.description: A Scottish nobleman who attends Duncan and helps escort the king to Macbeth's castle. Direct and principled in his first appearances, he belongs to the public order surrounding the monarchy.
characters.name: Macduff

characters.description: Banquo's young son, traveling with his father after dark at Macbeth's castle. His place in the family gives weight to the witches' prediction that Banquo will father kings.
characters.name: Fleance

characters.description: A Scottish nobleman who reports news from the battlefield and court. He becomes one of the figures through whom changes in loyalty, fear, and political control are made visible.
characters.name: Ross

characters.description: A Scottish nobleman in the royal circle who observes the aftermath of Duncan's visit. His formal questions and comments register the growing uncertainty within the court.
characters.name: Lennox

characters.description: Macduff's wife, left at the family home with their children. She feels exposed and abandoned by her husband's sudden departure, judging his political caution through its cost to the household.
characters.name: Lady Macduff

characters.description: The son of the English commander Siward, serving in the force that joins Malcolm's campaign. Young and eager to prove himself in combat, he represents the military support gathering against Macbeth.
characters.name: Young Siward

recaps.ending: Malcolm's army advances on Dunsinane with soldiers carrying branches cut from Birnam Wood, fulfilling the apparition's warning in a form Macbeth had assumed impossible. Macbeth learns that Lady Macbeth has died but continues to rely on the assurance that no man born in the ordinary way can harm him. In the battle he kills Young Siward and refuses to surrender. Macduff confronts him and reveals that he was delivered by surgical birth rather than born naturally. Macbeth understands that the witches' assurances were dangerously incomplete, yet fights and is killed. Macduff enters with Macbeth's severed head and hails Malcolm as king. Malcolm rewards his supporters, calls home the exiles who fled Macbeth's rule, and announces his coronation at Scone. Lady Macbeth's death, Banquo's murder, the destruction of Macduff's family, and Scotland's losses cannot be reversed, but Duncan's line is restored through Malcolm and Macbeth's violent reign ends.
recaps.in_short: After Scottish general Macbeth helps defeat a rebellion, three witches predict that he will gain a new title and become king, while Banquo's descendants will rule. The first prediction comes true at once. Encouraged by Lady Macbeth, Macbeth murders King Duncan during a royal visit and takes the crown, while Duncan's sons flee. Fearful of Banquo's prophecy, Macbeth has Banquo killed, though Fleance escapes, and Banquo's ghost exposes Macbeth's distress at a banquet. Further apparitions give Macbeth confidence through deceptive assurances. He orders the slaughter of Macduff's wife and children after Macduff joins Malcolm in England. Lady Macbeth, burdened by guilt, sleepwalks and later dies. Malcolm's army uses branches from Birnam Wood as camouflage while advancing on Dunsinane, fulfilling a warning Macbeth dismissed. Macduff, who was delivered by surgical birth, kills Macbeth. Malcolm becomes king and begins restoring Scotland after Macbeth's rule.

recaps.text: Scotland is fighting rebellion and foreign attack. King Duncan receives reports that Macbeth and Banquo have fought with exceptional courage, and he orders that Macbeth receive the title of the defeated Thane of Cawdor. Before the news reaches them, Macbeth and Banquo encounter three witches. They address Macbeth by his current title, by the title of Cawdor, and as a future king; they tell Banquo that his descendants will be kings though he will not. Ross and Angus then arrive and announce Macbeth's new title, making part of the prediction immediately true. Macbeth begins imagining the crown and is disturbed by the violent possibility that accompanies it. Duncan names his son Malcolm heir and plans to visit Macbeth's castle, placing both an obstacle and an opportunity before Macbeth.

Lady Macbeth reads her husband's account of the witches and fears he lacks the hardness to seize the crown. When Duncan's visit is announced, she resolves that he must not leave alive. Macbeth initially considers reasons against murder: Duncan is his king, relative, guest, and a good ruler, while Macbeth has no motive beyond ambition. Lady Macbeth attacks his courage and outlines a plan to intoxicate Duncan's guards, kill the sleeping king, and blame the servants. Macbeth agrees. Duncan arrives at the castle and is welcomed with formal loyalty, unaware of the plan. As the household settles for the night, Banquo tells Macbeth that he has dreamed of the witches. Macbeth conceals his thoughts and moves toward Duncan's room after imagining a dagger leading him there.

Macbeth murders Duncan but returns shaken, carrying the guards' daggers. Lady Macbeth takes the weapons back to the room and smears the sleeping guards with blood. Macduff discovers the king's body the next morning. Macbeth kills the guards, claiming rage, and Lady Macbeth diverts attention when his explanation draws scrutiny. Duncan's sons Malcolm and Donalbain fear a wider plot and flee separately, which makes them appear guilty. Macbeth is crowned at Scone. Banquo suspects that Macbeth gained the crown through murder but remembers that the witches promised kingship to his own descendants. Macduff avoids the coronation and returns home, a sign that acceptance of the new king is not complete. The natural and political order of Scotland has been disrupted, while Macbeth has obtained the position he and his wife sought.

As king, Macbeth fears Banquo's knowledge and the prophecy about Fleance. He hires murderers to attack father and son. Banquo is killed, but Fleance escapes. At a state banquet Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost occupying his place, though no one else can see it. His public terror disrupts the gathering, and Lady Macbeth dismisses the guests before he reveals more. Macbeth concludes that he must seek further knowledge from the witches and keep using violence to secure his position. Macduff has stayed away from the banquet and gone to England, where Malcolm is seeking support. Scottish nobles begin speaking cautiously about Macbeth as a tyrant and hope that Malcolm and Macduff can restore lawful government. Macbeth's crown is secure in appearance but increasingly dependent on fear, secrecy, and further killing.

The witches summon apparitions that warn Macbeth to beware Macduff, then tell him that no man born of woman will harm him and that he will remain safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane. A final vision shows Banquo's line continuing through future kings. Macbeth treats the apparently impossible conditions as guarantees, yet orders an immediate attack on Macduff's home. Murderers kill Lady Macduff and her children. In England, Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty by pretending to possess qualities that would make him an even worse ruler than Macbeth. Macduff's despair for Scotland convinces him, and Malcolm reveals that English forces are ready to help. Ross arrives with news of the slaughter at Macduff's castle. Macduff turns his grief toward the campaign against Macbeth, while Malcolm urges him to seek justice in battle.

Lady Macbeth sleepwalks under a doctor's observation, repeatedly acting as though she is washing blood from her hands and revealing the burden of remembered crimes. Malcolm, Macduff, and their allies advance toward Dunsinane. Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a branch from Birnam Wood and carry it as camouflage, making the wood appear to move. Macbeth remains confident in the witches' assurances even as supporters desert him. He receives news of Lady Macbeth's death and then hears that Birnam Wood seems to be advancing, forcing him to recognize that one prediction has turned against him. In battle Macbeth kills Young Siward, but Macduff seeks him personally. Macduff explains that he was delivered before natural birth; the assurance about ordinary birth therefore does not protect Macbeth. Macbeth fights and is killed. Macduff presents his head, Malcolm is acclaimed king, and the new ruler calls the exiles home and prepares for his coronation at Scone.

characters.description: The young son of the Montague household. At first absorbed in an unreturned infatuation, he is emotionally intense, impulsive, and more interested in love than in the street feud dividing Verona's leading families.
characters.name: Romeo Montague

characters.description: The only daughter of the Capulet household, not yet fourteen. Sheltered but observant, she initially treats marriage as a matter her parents may arrange and responds to their plans with courtesy rather than enthusiasm.
characters.name: Juliet Capulet

characters.description: Romeo's cousin and friend, a peaceable Montague who tries to stop the opening brawl. He listens sympathetically to Romeo's troubles and encourages him to look beyond his melancholy.
characters.name: Benvolio

characters.description: Juliet's hot-tempered Capulet cousin. Proud of his family and quick to interpret any Montague presence as an insult, he prefers combat to reconciliation.
characters.name: Tybalt

characters.description: Romeo's witty friend and a kinsman of Prince Escalus. Mercutio mocks romantic convention, delights in elaborate wordplay, and has little patience for Romeo's solemn approach to love.
characters.name: Mercutio

characters.description: The woman who raised Juliet from infancy and remains her intimate attendant. Talkative, earthy, and affectionate, she recalls Juliet's childhood in comic detail and acts as a practical intermediary between the girl and the adult world.
characters.name: The Nurse

characters.description: A Franciscan friar trusted by Romeo. He understands the intensity of youthful feeling but urges moderation, and he hopes that private goodwill might help end the public feud.
characters.name: Friar Lawrence

characters.description: The head of Juliet's household and an enemy of the Montagues. He can be a genial host, but he expects obedience in family matters and is highly sensitive to status and honor.
characters.name: Lord Capulet

characters.description: Juliet's mother, who presents Paris's marriage proposal to her daughter and assumes that an advantageous match is a natural part of Juliet's future.
characters.name: Lady Capulet

characters.description: Romeo's father and the head of the Montague household. He is concerned by his son's withdrawn behavior while remaining bound up in the longstanding feud with the Capulets.
characters.name: Lord Montague

characters.description: The ruler of Verona. Alarmed by repeated public violence between the Montagues and Capulets, he warns both households that further fighting will bring severe punishment.
characters.name: Prince Escalus

characters.description: A noble young kinsman of the prince who asks Lord Capulet for permission to marry Juliet. He approaches the match formally and has the approval of her parents.
characters.name: Count Paris

characters.description: A poor seller of medicines whom Romeo finds in Mantua. His desperate circumstances make him vulnerable to a request that the law forbids.
characters.name: The Apothecary

recaps.ending: Romeo reaches the Capulet tomb believing Juliet dead. He kills Paris when Paris confronts him there, then drinks poison beside Juliet's body. Juliet awakens after Friar Lawrence arrives, sees that Romeo is dead, and refuses to leave. When the friar flees at the sound of approaching guards, she kills herself with Romeo's dagger. The friar explains the secret marriage, the plan involving Juliet's sleeping potion, and the failed delivery of the message to Romeo. Evidence from Romeo's servant and letter confirms the account. Faced with the deaths caused by their hostility, Capulet and Montague reconcile and promise memorials to the young couple. Prince Escalus closes the inquiry by assigning shared responsibility: the families' feud, the lovers' desperate secrecy, and the adults' failures have turned an attempt at union into catastrophe.
recaps.in_short: In Verona, the Montagues and Capulets maintain a feud that repeatedly erupts into violence. Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet meet at a Capulet feast, fall in love, and marry secretly with Friar Lawrence's help. Soon afterward Tybalt kills Romeo's friend Mercutio, and Romeo kills Tybalt, leading to Romeo's banishment. Juliet's parents then order her to marry Paris. The friar gives Juliet a potion that will make her appear dead so that she can escape and reunite with Romeo, but the explanatory message never reaches him. Believing Juliet truly dead, Romeo buys poison and dies beside her in the family tomb. Juliet wakes, finds him dead, and kills herself. Friar Lawrence reveals the full story, and the grieving Montague and Capulet families finally end their feud.

recaps.text: A street quarrel between servants of the Montague and Capulet households grows into a public brawl. Prince Escalus stops it and declares that another outbreak will be punished severely. Romeo Montague has avoided the fighting because he is preoccupied with Rosaline, who does not return his love. Benvolio tries to lift his spirits. Meanwhile Count Paris asks Lord Capulet for Juliet's hand. Capulet invites him to a family feast, saying Juliet is still very young but allowing Paris to court her. A servant who cannot read asks Romeo for help with the guest list, unintentionally revealing the feast. Benvolio persuades Romeo to attend in disguise so he can compare Rosaline with other women. Lady Capulet and Juliet's Nurse tell Juliet about Paris's proposal. Juliet agrees to observe him but makes no promise beyond what her parents request.

Romeo enters the Capulet feast with Benvolio and Mercutio. There he sees Juliet and immediately forgets Rosaline. Tybalt recognizes Romeo's voice and wants to attack him, but Lord Capulet forbids violence under his roof. Romeo and Juliet speak, kiss, and only afterward learn that each belongs to the enemy family. Later Romeo slips into the Capulet orchard, where he hears Juliet privately confessing her love for him. He reveals himself, and they acknowledge that their family names make the relationship dangerous. Juliet insists that their vows must lead to honorable marriage rather than a passing courtship. They arrange for her to send a messenger to Romeo the next morning so he can provide the time and place for a wedding.

Friar Lawrence agrees to marry Romeo and Juliet, partly because their union might reconcile the two families. The Nurse carries messages between them, and the couple marry in secret. Soon afterward Tybalt challenges Romeo. Bound to Tybalt by the hidden marriage, Romeo refuses to fight, but Mercutio takes up the challenge and is fatally wounded when Romeo intervenes. Enraged and grieving, Romeo kills Tybalt. Prince Escalus spares Romeo's life but banishes him from Verona. Juliet first reacts with horror to the news of Tybalt's death, then remains loyal to her husband. The Nurse helps Romeo reach Juliet for a final night together before he must leave for Mantua, while Friar Lawrence urges him to wait there for a chance to disclose the marriage and seek a pardon.

After Romeo departs, Juliet's parents attempt to relieve what they think is grief for Tybalt by arranging her rapid marriage to Paris. Juliet refuses. Lord Capulet responds with threats of rejection, Lady Capulet offers no protection, and even the Nurse advises Juliet to forget the banished Romeo and accept Paris. Feeling abandoned, Juliet goes to Friar Lawrence. He proposes a dangerous escape: she will drink a potion that produces the appearance of death, be placed in the Capulet tomb, and awaken after roughly two days. The friar will send Romeo an explanation so that Romeo can retrieve her and take her away. Juliet accepts, returns home, pretends to consent to the wedding, and drinks the potion despite fears about its effects and the tomb.

The Nurse finds Juliet unresponsive on the morning planned for her wedding. The Capulet household's preparations turn into funeral arrangements, and Juliet is carried to the family tomb. Friar Lawrence's message to Romeo fails because the messenger is prevented from completing the journey. Romeo instead hears from his servant Balthasar that Juliet is dead. With no knowledge of the potion plan, he resolves to die beside her. In Mantua he finds an impoverished apothecary and persuades him to sell a lethal poison. Romeo then returns secretly to Verona, carrying the means to kill himself and a letter explaining his intentions.

At the Capulet tomb, Paris confronts Romeo and is killed in the ensuing fight. Romeo enters, says farewell to Juliet, and drinks poison. Friar Lawrence arrives as Juliet wakes, but Romeo is already dead. The friar urges her to flee, then leaves when guards approach; Juliet remains and kills herself with Romeo's dagger. The prince, the Capulets, and the Montagues gather to investigate. Friar Lawrence recounts the lovers' marriage, Romeo's banishment, Juliet's potion, and the message that failed to reach Mantua. Supporting testimony and Romeo's letter confirm the sequence. The deaths expose the final cost of the feud. Capulet and Montague reconcile and promise to honor Romeo and Juliet with memorials, while Prince Escalus declares that the disaster has punished all involved.

characters.description: The ruler of Illyria, absorbed in his love for the wealthy Countess Olivia despite her refusal to receive him. He sends messengers to press his courtship and enjoys cultivating an atmosphere of music and romantic longing.
characters.name: Orsino

characters.description: A young gentlewoman rescued after a shipwreck on the coast of Illyria. Believing her twin brother Sebastian drowned and needing protection in an unfamiliar country, she disguises herself as a young man called Cesario and seeks employment in Orsino's household.
characters.name: Viola

characters.description: A seaman who rescues Viola after the wreck. He explains the political and social situation in Illyria and agrees to help her assume a male disguise, keeping her identity secret while she enters Orsino's service.
characters.name: Sea Captain

characters.description: Olivia's uncle, a convivial and disorderly resident of her household. He stays up drinking, resents restraint, and encourages Sir Andrew's courtship partly because Andrew's money supports their entertainment.
characters.name: Sir Toby Belch

characters.description: Olivia's practical waiting-gentlewoman. She trades sharp remarks with Sir Toby, criticizes his disruptive habits, and is comfortable enough in the household to challenge both servants and their social superiors.
characters.name: Maria

characters.description: A wealthy but foolish knight staying with Sir Toby in hopes of marrying Olivia. Easily flattered and discouraged, he boasts of accomplishments he cannot convincingly demonstrate and supplies money for Sir Toby's revels.
characters.name: Sir Andrew Aguecheek

characters.description: A wealthy countess mourning her dead brother and refusing Orsino's courtship. She intends to withdraw from society for years, though the arrival of Orsino's unusually eloquent new messenger soon unsettles that resolve.
characters.name: Olivia

characters.description: Olivia's steward, a grave and self-important servant who disapproves of the late-night pleasures of Sir Toby and his companions. He values order and takes pride in his own dignity and judgment.
characters.name: Malvolio

characters.description: Olivia's licensed fool, a singer and quick verbal performer whose apparent nonsense often exposes the folly of people with higher status. He has been absent from the household and must talk his way back into Olivia's favor.
characters.name: Feste

characters.description: Viola's twin brother, who also survives the shipwreck but believes Viola has drowned. Grief-stricken yet determined to travel on through Illyria, he resembles his sister closely enough that her male disguise makes the two nearly indistinguishable to strangers.
characters.name: Sebastian

characters.description: A sea captain who rescues Sebastian and becomes devoted to him. Although he has dangerous enemies in Orsino's territory because of an earlier naval conflict, he is reluctant to let Sebastian face Illyria alone.
characters.name: Antonio

characters.description: A gentleman serving Olivia who resents Malvolio for interfering with the household's amusements. He joins Sir Toby and Sir Andrew in hiding nearby while Malvolio discovers Maria's forged letter.
characters.name: Fabian

recaps.ending: In the final gathering, Sebastian's appearance proves that he and Viola are separate people and resolves the many mistakes caused by their resemblance. The twins recognize each other and rejoice that both survived the shipwreck. Olivia accepts that she has married Sebastian rather than Cesario, while Orsino learns that Cesario is Viola and turns his affection toward her; Viola will resume her female clothing once it is recovered. Maria's forged letter is exposed as the cause of Malvolio's humiliation. Sir Toby has married Maria, but Malvolio leaves vowing retaliation against the household. Orsino orders that he be pursued and reconciled if possible. The play closes with two newly acknowledged couples, Olivia and Sebastian and Orsino and Viola, while Feste remains to sing about the persistence of ordinary hardship beyond the festivities.
recaps.in_short: After a shipwreck separates twins Viola and Sebastian, Viola disguises herself as a young man named Cesario and serves Duke Orsino, who sends her to court the mourning Countess Olivia. Viola falls for Orsino, while Olivia falls for Cesario. In Olivia's household, Maria, Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, Fabian, and Feste punish the pompous steward Malvolio with a forged letter that persuades him Olivia loves him. Sebastian, also alive, enters Illyria with the loyal Antonio. Because he looks like the disguised Viola, he is mistaken for Cesario, accepts Olivia's sudden proposal, and baffles people involved in Sir Andrew's challenge. The confusions converge when both twins appear together. Viola reveals her identity; Orsino recognizes his love for her, and Olivia remains happily married to Sebastian. The prank on Malvolio is confessed, and he departs angrily while the household celebrates the paired marriages.

recaps.text: Duke Orsino of Illyria longs for Countess Olivia, who has withdrawn from courtship while mourning her brother. On the coast, Viola survives a shipwreck but believes her twin brother Sebastian has died. With a sea captain's help, she adopts male clothing and the name Cesario so she can safely enter Orsino's service. Elsewhere, Olivia's uncle Sir Toby drinks and makes noise in her house with Sir Andrew Aguecheek, a rich, inept suitor whom he encourages to keep pursuing Olivia. Maria, Olivia's waiting-gentlewoman, warns them that their conduct is unwelcome. Viola quickly gains Orsino's confidence. He sends Cesario to present his love to Olivia, while Viola privately realizes that she has fallen in love with Orsino herself.

Cesario gains an audience with Olivia and speaks for Orsino with such force that Olivia becomes interested in the messenger instead of the master. She sends Malvolio after Cesario with a ring and pretends it was left behind. Viola understands that Olivia has fallen for her male disguise and sees the emerging triangle: she loves Orsino, Orsino loves Olivia, and Olivia loves Cesario. Meanwhile, Sebastian is revealed to have survived the wreck. He believes Viola dead and prepares to travel into Illyria. Antonio, the captain who rescued him, cares for him deeply and decides to follow despite having enemies in Orsino's territory.

Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, and Feste hold a loud late-night gathering until Malvolio rebukes them and threatens to report Maria. In response, Maria devises a punishment based on Malvolio's vanity: she will imitate Olivia's handwriting in a letter suggesting that Olivia secretly loves him and wants him to behave in a series of conspicuous ways. Orsino continues confiding in Cesario about love. Viola comes close to describing her own feelings but cannot reveal her identity. At Olivia's house, Malvolio finds the planted letter while Maria and the others watch from hiding. He convinces himself it is genuine and resolves to approach Olivia smiling, wearing yellow stockings crossed with garters, and treating the rest of the household with arrogance. The tricksters are delighted that he has followed their design.

Olivia declares her love directly to Cesario, but Viola can only reject her. Sir Andrew decides to leave because Olivia favors the page; Sir Toby keeps him present by persuading him to challenge Cesario. Antonio catches up with Sebastian and gives him money before they separate to explore the town. Malvolio then appears before Olivia in the bizarre clothing and manner prescribed by the forged letter. Because Olivia knows nothing of the trick, she thinks he is mentally unwell and leaves Sir Toby to supervise him. Maria and her companions intensify the deception by treating Malvolio as possessed. At the same time, Sir Toby and Fabian frighten both Sir Andrew and the equally unwilling Cesario with exaggerated accounts of the other's skill in combat, forcing them toward a duel neither wants.

Antonio mistakes Cesario for Sebastian and intervenes in the duel. When officers arrest him, he asks for the money he gave Sebastian, but Viola cannot understand him and has none. Antonio interprets this as betrayal. His references to Sebastian give Viola hope that her brother may be alive. Sebastian then arrives and is repeatedly mistaken for Cesario. Unlike Viola, he responds forcefully when Sir Andrew and Sir Toby attack him. Olivia intervenes, addresses him as Cesario, and urges him to come with her. Though astonished by her affection and by the strange familiarity of everyone around him, Sebastian accepts the good fortune and agrees to marry her. Malvolio has meanwhile been confined in darkness. Feste disguises his voice as a learned examiner to torment him, then promises to carry out a letter in which Malvolio asks Olivia for release.

Orsino visits Olivia with Cesario. Olivia treats Cesario as her husband, while Antonio identifies the page as Sebastian, producing accusations of betrayal on every side. Sir Andrew and Sir Toby enter wounded and blame Cesario for beating them. The appearance of the real Sebastian finally separates the two identities. Sebastian and Viola recognize one another as the twins lost in the wreck, and Viola explains her disguise. Olivia accepts Sebastian as the man she married. Orsino, seeing that Cesario is Viola and recalling her devotion, asks Viola to become his wife once she resumes her own identity. Feste delivers Malvolio's letter, and Malvolio is released. Fabian and Feste explain Maria's forged message; Fabian also reports that Sir Toby has married Maria. Malvolio leaves in anger, promising revenge, while Orsino calls for an effort to make peace and prepares for the two marriages.

characters.description: The head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, the Soviet officer who ran the agent that destroyed the Circus and who has been Smiley's opponent for twenty years. He is known to the British only by a work name, a photograph and a career reconstructed from fragments: ascetic, unbribable, and safe from the ordinary levers because he appears to want nothing for himself. Smiley met him once, years ago, in an Indian jail, tried to turn him and failed, and gave him a cigarette lighter belonging to his wife.
characters.name: Karla

characters.description: A Russian emigree living in modest circumstances in Paris, ageing, unwell and alone, who left the Soviet Union many years ago and had to leave a daughter behind. She is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who offers, on conditions, to have the girl allowed out to join her. Suspicious of the offer and of the papers she is asked to sign, she writes for advice to the leader of an emigre organisation she trusted long ago.
characters.name: Maria Ostrakova

characters.description: The Soviet official who approaches Ostrakova in Paris: nominally a trade or embassy functionary, effusive, sweating and oddly clumsy for a man on such an errand. He talks a great deal more than his business requires.
characters.name: Oleg Kirov

characters.description: An elderly Estonian, once a soldier and a Soviet officer and for decades afterwards the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London, run for years as a Circus agent and then dropped when the service reorganised. Poor, proud and still observing the tradecraft he was taught, he telephones his old service demanding to speak to the case officer he knew by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has something that concerns them all.
characters.name: General Vladimir

characters.description: Long retired from the Circus, living alone in Chelsea and sorting his papers, still married in name to Ann and still without her. He is fetched out at night to deal with the death of a former agent, on the understanding that his job is to tidy the matter away quietly. He is old, tired and out of practice, and the one man who understands what the dead man was trying to say.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: Smiley's wife, absent, living elsewhere with someone else, and still the fixed point of his private life. Her cigarette lighter and her infidelities both belong to the history that binds Smiley to his opponent.
characters.name: Ann Smiley

characters.description: The Cabinet Office official responsible for the intelligence services, anxious above all that an emigre killing in London should not become a political embarrassment. He wants the affair closed with a minimum of enquiry and turns to Smiley because Smiley can be disowned.
characters.name: Oliver Lacon

characters.description: A senior Circus administrator of the present regime, protective of procedure, budgets and his own position, who treats the dead man as an obsolete liability and Smiley as an awkwardness to be managed.
characters.name: Lauder Strickland

characters.description: A very young Circus duty officer who took the old man's telephone call and, having been taught nothing about the people the service used to run, handled it by the book. He is shaken by what followed and tells Smiley more than he is supposed to.
characters.name: Mostyn

characters.description: An Estonian exile who runs a Baltic emigre library and club in London, once the General's deputy and now the keeper of his organisation's dwindling affairs. Talkative, aggrieved and a considerable chess player, he gives his own version of the old man's last weeks.
characters.name: Mikhel

characters.description: A young Estonian lorry driver on the continental routes, the son of one of the General's old comrades, who ran errands for the old man out of family loyalty and without understanding what he was carrying. He is frightened and wants nothing more to do with any of it.
characters.name: Villem

characters.description: The Circus's former Soviet researcher, now seriously ill and living in the Norfolk countryside with her companion and her dogs, drinking and remembering. Her memory for Moscow Centre's people and their careers is still complete, and she has never stopped following the career of one officer in particular.
characters.name: Connie Sachs

characters.description: A stateless adventurer of Baltic origin, sometime prisoner, confidence man and agent for several services, who worked with the General for years. Charming, unreliable and physically brave, he lives in Hamburg and has been chasing a particular Soviet official for reasons of his own.
characters.name: Otto Leipzig

characters.description: A former Circus officer, now dealing in pictures in the West End under an assumed name and a foreign accent. Hungarian, adaptable and expert in surveillance and safe houses, he owes Smiley his freedom from prosecution and comes back to run a team for him without asking what the operation is for.
characters.name: Toby Esterhase

characters.description: A Hamburg nightclub proprietor and old associate of Otto Leipzig, discreet, businesslike and loyal to his friend. He keeps what Leipzig left with him and will hand it over only on the right terms.
characters.name: Claus Kretzschmar

characters.description: The commercial counsellor at the Soviet embassy in Bern, a pedantic, henpecked official with an academic manner, a wife who watches him and a mistress among the embassy staff. He performs, under orders from Moscow, a private duty outside all normal embassy business, and he is very frightened of it.
characters.name: Grigoriev

characters.description: A young Russian woman in a private Swiss clinic, disturbed, articulate and intermittently violent, held under a name and a nationality that are not hers. She does not know who is paying for her, and the accounts she gives of her own history contradict one another.
characters.name: Alexandra

recaps.ending: Grigoriev, broken by Toby's team and questioned by Smiley in a Bern safe flat, gives up the whole arrangement: the girl in the clinic is Karla's daughter, mentally ill, smuggled out of Russia under a false identity and a false nationality, and maintained in Switzerland with money embezzled from Moscow Centre's operational funds. Kirov was ordered to build the legend, talked too much to Otto Leipzig, and was recalled and shot; Vladimir, Leipzig and very nearly Ostrakova were killed to bury the same secret. Smiley now has what no professional lever could give him: the private crime for which Karla's own service would destroy him. He sends word to Moscow through the channel Karla built, offering him the choice between exposure and coming across. Karla comes. On a bridge in Berlin, watched by Smiley, Toby and the reception party, he crosses into the West, a small man carrying almost nothing, and as he passes he drops the cigarette lighter Smiley once gave him. Smiley has beaten him by using the one human attachment Karla had, exactly as Karla would have done, and the victory gives him nothing. He turns away, and when Toby tells him he has won he can barely agree.
recaps.in_short: In Paris an ageing Russian emigree, Ostrakova, is approached by a Soviet official offering to release the daughter she left behind, and writes for help to General Vladimir, an old Estonian exile in London and a discarded Circus agent. Vladimir tries to reach his former case officer under Moscow rules and is shot dead on Hampstead Heath. Smiley, long retired, is sent to tidy the death away quietly, and instead follows the trail the old man left: a hidden negative, an emigre courier, a Hamburg confidence man named Otto Leipzig, and photographs and a tape recording of the Soviet official's indiscretions. Reassembling his old people, Connie Sachs, Toby Esterhase, Guillam and Mendel, and working outside the service, Smiley establishes that Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, has been using Centre money and Centre officers to hide his mentally ill daughter in a Swiss clinic under a false identity. Everyone who learned of it has been killed. Smiley breaks the Soviet official who pays the clinic's bills, and uses the daughter to force Karla's defection. Karla crosses a Berlin bridge into the West, and Smiley takes no pleasure in it.

recaps.text: Previously: George Smiley spent his career in the Circus, Britain's secret intelligence service, and much of it against Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate. Karla recruited and ran Bill Haydon, who rose to the top of the Circus, betrayed its networks and its allies, wrecked the operation that left Jim Prideaux shot and imprisoned, and conducted an affair with Smiley's wife Ann on Karla's instructions to blunt Smiley's judgement. Brought back from retirement, Smiley identified and trapped Haydon and was left to rebuild the ruined service. Working backwards through what Haydon had suppressed, he then uncovered a Soviet payments operation in the Far East and traced it to Nelson Ko, an agent Karla had run inside China for twenty years; but the prize was taken over by the Americans and by Whitehall, the field man Jerry Westerby was killed, and Smiley was eased out of the chief's chair in favour of Saul Enderby. Smiley's marriage to Ann has not survived, and the two men's twenty-year contest has never been settled.

In Paris, Maria Ostrakova, an ageing Russian emigree, is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who says her daughter Alexandra, left behind in Russia many years earlier, may be allowed to join her if she signs certain papers. The interview frightens her: the man knows too much about her history and too little about her daughter, and the arrangement smells of something other than compassion. She writes to General Vladimir, the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London whom she trusted long ago. Vladimir, an old Estonian long since dropped by the Circus, telephones his former service demanding to see the case officer he knew only by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has proof of something big. A young duty officer handles the call by the book. Before any meeting can take place, Vladimir is shot dead on Hampstead Heath at night, his face destroyed by the second bullet, and George Smiley is fetched out of retirement to identify the body.

Lacon of the Cabinet Office and the Circus administrator Strickland want the killing disposed of as an emigre quarrel with no British connection, and give Smiley an unofficial commission to make the loose ends disappear. Smiley does the opposite. Going over the old man's route and lodgings, he finds what the killers missed: a cigarette packet left in the classic manner with a photographic negative concealed in it, the proof Vladimir was carrying to his meeting. He interviews the young duty officer, who repeats the old man's words; and Mikhel, the deputy at the emigre library, whose account is fluent and incomplete. He learns that Vladimir had recently sent a young Estonian courier abroad. The service, meanwhile, formally wants nothing to do with any of it, which leaves Smiley free to work alone.

The courier, a lorry driver named Villem, admits to a run to Hamburg where a stranger passed him an envelope on a train. Smiley goes to Norfolk to see Connie Sachs, dying and drinking in the country, who identifies the men in the story: Otto Leipzig, a Baltic adventurer and part-time agent who had worked with Vladimir for years, and Oleg Kirov, a Soviet official whose career and postings make no sense unless he was doing something outside embassy work. Connie also confirms whose directorate Kirov belonged to. In Hamburg, Smiley finds that Leipzig has been murdered, but recovers from Leipzig's associate Kretzschmar what the operation was for: a compromising photograph and a tape on which Kirov, drunk and boastful, describes having been ordered to find a suitable emigre identity for a girl, a piece of work no intelligence service would ever run in that way.

Smiley recruits his own people rather than the Circus's: Toby Esterhase, now selling pictures in the West End, brings a surveillance team; Peter Guillam helps from Paris; Mendel does the London work. In Paris, Ostrakova, who has been living in fear since the approach, is run down in the street and badly hurt, and survives; Smiley finds her and hears her account of Kirov's proposition and of the daughter she has not seen since infancy. The pattern is now clear. Kirov was building a false identity in the West for a young woman, using an emigree mother as the cover story, and everyone who came near the secret has been killed: Kirov himself recalled to Moscow and shot, then Vladimir and Leipzig. The operation was not run by Moscow Centre as an institution but by one man inside it, using its resources for a purpose of his own, and the trail leads to Switzerland.

In Bern, Toby's team identifies the man who does the paying: Grigoriev, the Soviet embassy's commercial counsellor, a fussy, unhappy official who makes regular private journeys to a discreet clinic in the countryside and hands over large sums in cash. In the clinic is a disturbed young Russian woman, registered under a name and a nationality that are not hers, who does not know who is responsible for her. Smiley has the watchers document every movement, then has Grigoriev taken quietly and confronted in a safe flat with what has been observed: the money, the false papers, his mistress, and the certainty that his own service would treat all of it as a capital matter. Grigoriev, terrified and relieved to be able to speak, begins to explain who ordered him to do it and why.

Grigoriev's account completes the case: the girl in the clinic is Karla's own daughter, mentally ill, taken out of Russia under an invented identity and kept in Switzerland with money stolen from Moscow Centre's operational funds. It is the one act for which Karla's own service would destroy him, and it is why Kirov, Vladimir and Leipzig died and why Ostrakova was to have died. Smiley sends Karla the choice through the channel Karla himself built: come over, or be exposed to Moscow. Then he waits in Berlin. On a winter night Karla walks across the bridge into the West, a small, ordinary man carrying nothing, and as he passes Smiley he drops the cigarette lighter that Smiley had given him twenty years earlier in an Indian jail. Smiley has won by doing exactly what his opponent would have done, using a sick girl and a frightened official as instruments, and he leaves the bridge with no sense of triumph at all.

characters.description: Fourteen, and pulled out of the sea off the Australian coast after falling back to Earth from orbit. He is exhausted, a long way from home and, for once, in the hands of a service that has no file on him and no claim over him. That does not last.
characters.name: Alex Rider

characters.description: A senior officer of the Australian Secret Intelligence Service, direct and persuasive, who has been trying for years to get somebody inside the people-smuggling networks that run through Southeast Asia. He knows precisely who Alex is by the time they meet, and he has a proposal ready.
characters.name: Ethan Brooke

characters.description: A former MI6 officer, now with the Australian service, who turns out to be Alex's godfather. He worked alongside John and Helen Rider, was there the night Alex's life changed, and carries a bad old wound in his stomach from it. He is the first person Alex has met who knew his parents as people rather than as files, and he is to travel with Alex as his minder.
characters.name: Ash

characters.description: The head of a snakehead operating out of Bangkok, half English and half Chinese, educated at an English public school and impeccably polite about it. He suffers from a bone disease that makes his skeleton brittle, so he moves carefully and is never without protection, and he runs a business that moves human beings as freight and sells whatever is left of them.
characters.name: Major Winston Yu

characters.description: The MI6 agent Alex first met under the codename Fox during Special Air Service selection training. Young, capable and one of the few people in the service who treats Alex as a colleague, he arrives as part of the operation's back-up.
characters.name: Ben Daniels

characters.description: The deputy head of MI6 Special Operations, who knows more about what happened to Alex's parents than she has ever been willing to say.
characters.name: Mrs Jones

recaps.ending: The bomb is stopped: Alex prevents Royal Blue from triggering the landslide, no wave is generated, and the conference and the coastline are never hit. Major Winston Yu does not survive the operation, and the snakehead's network is broken open. The harder ending is Ash. Alex learns that his godfather was the traitor inside the operation years ago, the man Scorpia paid to betray John Rider and to make sure the Riders' plane came down; Alex's parents died because Ash sold them. Ash is fatally injured during the fighting, and dies having admitted it, leaving Alex with a truth that nobody else needs and no one to be angry at. Alex goes home to London knowing exactly how his mother and father died and who arranged it, having been used again by a service that is not even his own, and having been closer to being killed on an operating table than in any firefight. Scorpia, whose contract set the whole thing in motion, remains in business.
recaps.in_short: Fished out of the sea off Australia after his fall from orbit, Alex is recruited by the Australian Secret Intelligence Service to go into the snakeheads, the gangs that smuggle people across Southeast Asia. He is teamed with Ash, a former MI6 officer who turns out to be his godfather and who knew his parents. Posing as refugees, the two are moved along the smuggling route to a camp where the gang's other trade becomes clear: those who cannot pay are taken to an illegal clinic and stripped for organs, and Alex is nearly killed on the table. Captured, he is brought before Major Winston Yu, who runs the operation and has taken a contract from Scorpia called Royal Blue: a bomb sunk at an unstable point on the seabed to trigger an underwater landslide and a wave that would destroy an international aid conference and the coast around it. Alex stops the detonation and Yu is killed. He also learns that Ash was the traitor who betrayed his parents to Scorpia; Ash dies admitting it.

recaps.text: Previously: Alex Rider, fourteen, was recruited by MI6 after his uncle Ian's murder and used repeatedly by Alan Blunt and Mrs Jones. He stopped Herod Sayle's poisoned school computers, broke Dr Hugo Grief's cloning operation at Point Blanc, survived General Alexei Sarov, and prevented Damian Cray from launching stolen American missiles; the dying assassin Yassen Gregorovich sent him to Venice, where Scorpia's Julia Rothman recruited him with a lie about his father before he discovered the organisation meant to murder thousands of London schoolchildren and destroyed its weapon. MI6 then told him the truth: John Rider had been their own officer, working inside Scorpia under the codename Hunter, and his execution was staged to bring him out. Alex's parents died soon afterwards when a bomb brought down their plane. Scorpia's answer to Alex was a sniper's bullet in the chest. Most recently, the billionaire Nikolai Drevin tried to bring his own space station down on Washington; Alex diverted it and fell back to Earth into the sea off Australia.

Alex comes down in the ocean off the Australian coast and is picked up alive. Instead of being sent straight home he is passed to the Australian Secret Intelligence Service, whose senior officer Ethan Brooke has a proposal. The service has spent years failing to get anyone inside the snakeheads, the gangs that move people illegally across Southeast Asia and treat them as cargo, and a boy travelling with an adult would be exactly the kind of pair the route swallows without comment. The adult offered to Alex is Ash: a former MI6 officer, now working in Australia, who was a friend and colleague of John and Helen Rider and who is Alex's godfather. It is the first time Alex has met anybody who knew his parents personally.

Alex and Ash go in as a father and son with no money and no papers, and are handed along the snakehead's chain from Bangkok southward. Ash talks, guardedly, about the Riders, and about the night Alex's life changed and the wound he still carries from it, but there is a great deal he will not say. The journey itself is worse than either of them expected: the people around them have paid everything they have for a passage that treats them as freight, the handlers are casual about who arrives and who does not, and there is no way to leave the route once you are on it.

The route ends not in a new country but at a holding camp, and there Alex discovers the snakehead's second trade. Those who cannot pay the rest of their passage are taken to an illegal clinic run for the organisation, where they are used as a source of organs for buyers who ask no questions. Alex is identified as a healthy donor and taken to the table, and comes closer to being killed there than in any operation he has run. He gets off it and out of the camp, but he can no longer pretend to be a refugee, and the people running the network now know that somebody has been inside it.

Alex is taken to Major Winston Yu, who owns the snakehead: a courteous, English-educated man whose bones are so brittle that a fall would cripple him, and who describes his business as logistics. Yu is not working for himself. Scorpia has bought his network for an operation called Royal Blue, and the target is an international aid conference being held off the Australian coast, where the people the client wants dead will be gathered in one place. The method is geological. A bomb sunk at a precise point on the seabed will bring down an unstable shelf, and the wave it raises will do the killing, leaving a natural disaster and no assassin to find.
