The bomb is already in place on a disused offshore platform, with the timing set and the conference assembling. Alex reaches the rig with the operation's back-up, including Ben Daniels, the MI6 agent he first knew as Fox at the SAS training camp. In the fighting on the platform Alex stops the detonation; there is no landslide and no wave, the conference and the coast are untouched, and Major Yu does not survive. The snakehead's network is broken open, though Scorpia, which commissioned the whole thing, is not touched at all.

The last thing Alex learns is the worst. Ash was the traitor. Years earlier, in the operation that ended his own career, he took Scorpia's money and gave them John Rider, and it was Ash who made sure the plane carrying Alex's parents came down. His godfather is the reason Alex grew up without them. Ash is fatally injured in the fighting on the rig and dies having admitted all of it, leaving Alex holding a confession nobody else has any use for. Alex goes home to London knowing exactly how his mother and father died and who arranged it, having been lent out, used and very nearly killed by a service that was not even his own.

characters.description: A Japanese American fisherman on trial for the murder of Carl Heine. Kabuo is a husband and father whose rigid stillness in court gives observers little indication of what he is thinking.
characters.name: Kabuo Miyamoto

characters.description: Kabuo's wife, seated behind him during the trial. Hatsue is composed and attentive as she follows the proceedings that will decide whether her husband returns to their family.
characters.name: Hatsue Miyamoto

characters.description: The editor and sole reporter of the island newspaper, attending Kabuo's trial as both journalist and local observer. A wounded veteran who lost an arm in the war, Ishmael is watchful and emotionally withdrawn.
characters.name: Ishmael Chambers

characters.description: The dead fisherman whose body was pulled from his own net. Carl was a large, quiet islander, a husband and father, and an experienced seaman whose apparent drowning begins to look suspicious.
characters.name: Carl Heine Jr.

characters.description: San Piedro's sheriff, responsible for investigating Carl Heine's death. Art is methodical and generally decent, but the unusual wound on Carl's head and other circumstantial clues lead him to treat the drowning as a possible homicide.
characters.name: Art Moran

characters.description: Carl's widow and the mother of his children. Grieving but direct, Susan Marie helps Sheriff Moran establish her husband's habits and movements around the time of his death.
characters.name: Susan Marie Heine

characters.description: The prosecutor in Kabuo's trial. Hooks builds a case from physical traces, the Miyamoto family's land grievance, and Kabuo's initial lack of candor, presenting separate pieces of circumstantial evidence as a single deliberate killing.
characters.name: Alvin Hooks

characters.description: Kabuo's elderly defense attorney. Gudmundsson challenges the prosecution's assumptions and warns the jury against allowing racial stereotypes or Kabuo's controlled expression to substitute for proof.
characters.name: Nels Gudmundsson

characters.description: The island coroner, who examines Carl's body. Whaley identifies a head injury that occurred before the drowning and recognizes that its shape could be consistent with a forceful blow, an observation that helps turn an apparent fishing accident into a murder inquiry.
characters.name: Horace Whaley

characters.description: Carl's mother, a stern woman who never accepted the Miyamoto family's claim on land once owned by the Heines. During the wartime removal, she used the missed payments to end the Miyamotos' purchase agreement and later sold the farm elsewhere.
characters.name: Etta Heine

characters.description: Kabuo's father, who arranged to buy strawberry acreage from Carl Heine Sr. and improved it while making payments. The wartime incarceration of his family prevented him from completing the agreement, leaving Kabuo determined to recover what he regards as the family's land.
characters.name: Zenhichi Miyamoto

characters.description: Ishmael's late father and the former editor of the island newspaper. Arthur reported firmly against anti-Japanese agitation and taught his son that a local newspaper owes its community fairness as well as facts.
characters.name: Arthur Chambers

recaps.ending: Ishmael finds records from the lighthouse radio station showing that a freighter passed San Piedro during the fogbound night of Carl's death. Its wake, arriving during a local power failure, explains how Carl could have been knocked from his boat after climbing the mast to deal with his lantern. The evidence supports Kabuo's account of helping Carl with a dead battery and then leaving him alive. Ishmael initially sits alone with information that can save the husband of the woman he still loves, but Hatsue's appeal to his better nature ends his hesitation. He gives her the records, and she takes them to Sheriff Moran. The authorities confirm the accident and the charge against Kabuo is dismissed before the jury delivers a verdict. Kabuo returns to Hatsue and their children. Hatsue remains grateful to Ishmael but does not renew their youthful romance; her life is with Kabuo. By choosing truth over resentment, Ishmael begins to move beyond the grievance that has governed his postwar life and writes the full account of Carl's accidental death.
recaps.in_short: In 1954, Japanese American fisherman Kabuo Miyamoto stands trial on San Piedro Island for killing fellow fisherman Carl Heine. The prosecution links a head wound, blood and a disputed boat battery to an old conflict over strawberry land that Kabuo's family lost while incarcerated during World War II. The trial draws out the island's buried history: prejudice against its Japanese American residents, Kabuo's war service, and newspaper editor Ishmael Chambers's secret youthful love for Kabuo's wife, Hatsue. Kabuo eventually explains that he found Carl disabled at sea, helped him install a spare battery, discussed buying back the family acreage, and left him alive. Ishmael discovers lighthouse records proving that a freighter's wake could have knocked Carl from his mast during a power failure. After briefly withholding the evidence, Ishmael gives it to Hatsue. The accident is confirmed, Kabuo is freed, and Ishmael finally acts according to the fairness his father taught him rather than the bitterness he has carried since the war and Hatsue's rejection.

recaps.text: A winter storm surrounds the courthouse on San Piedro Island as Kabuo Miyamoto, a Japanese American fisherman, goes on trial for murdering Carl Heine Jr. Carl's body had been found caught in his own fishing net after his boat was discovered drifting. Sheriff Art Moran's investigation showed that Carl suffered a serious head injury before drowning, making an ordinary accident seem doubtful. The courtroom brings together people whose histories are deeply connected: Kabuo's wife Hatsue; Ishmael Chambers, the island newspaper editor and a wounded war veteran; Carl's widow Susan Marie; and the attorneys Alvin Hooks and Nels Gudmundsson. From the outset, the case rests on interpretation as much as direct evidence. Kabuo's controlled expression looks suspicious to some observers, while his defense insists that reserve and ancestry are not proof of violence.

The coroner testifies that Carl's head wound was inflicted before he entered the water and could match a forceful strike. Investigators also focus on a battery associated with Carl's boat and on physical traces that may place Kabuo aboard it. The prosecution begins arranging these facts into a theory of murder, although no witness saw Carl die. Alongside the courtroom evidence, the story returns to Ishmael and Hatsue's childhood. They grew close while young but concealed the relationship because Hatsue expected her family and the island to reject it. Their private bond gives Ishmael's coverage of the trial a personal stake he cannot acknowledge publicly. Hatsue is now committed to Kabuo and their children, while Ishmael's wartime injury and unresolved longing have left him detached from much of island life.

The alleged motive reaches back to land. Kabuo's father, Zenhichi, had made payments to Carl Heine Sr. for strawberry acreage and worked the property for years. When the government removed the island's Japanese American families during World War II, the Miyamotos could no longer maintain the agreement. Etta Heine ended the arrangement and later sold the farm to another buyer. Kabuo returned from military service believing that his family had been deprived of land they had nearly paid for, and he continued trying to recover it. The trial also exposes how readily old racial hostility can color neutral facts. Ishmael remembers his father Arthur using the island newspaper to oppose such prejudice. Those memories sharpen the contrast between the public duty Ishmael inherited and the private resentment he still carries toward Hatsue.

The past of the principal witnesses becomes inseparable from the trial. Hatsue's family was sent away from the island and eventually confined at Manzanar. Under pressure from her family, her own doubts, and the upheaval of removal, she ended her hidden relationship with Ishmael and later married Kabuo. Both men then fought in the war: Ishmael returned missing an arm, and Kabuo returned burdened by what he had done as a soldier. Carl likewise came home changed. The prosecution treats Kabuo's land grievance and martial skill as evidence of a planned attack, while the defense argues that war, reserve, and anger do not establish murder. Testimony about the boats and the blood evidence strengthens the circumstantial case, but the exact sequence on the water remains unknown.

Kabuo explains why he initially concealed part of the night from Sheriff Moran. He says he encountered Carl at sea with a dead battery and supplied a compatible spare. While the men worked aboard Carl's boat, Kabuo cut his hand, accounting for his blood there. They also spoke about the Heine acreage, and Carl agreed in principle to sell Kabuo the portion his family had once sought. Kabuo then left Carl alive. He withheld the meeting because he understood how the land dispute, his presence on the boat, and local prejudice would make the truth sound like a murder story. His testimony offers an innocent explanation for the physical evidence, but it also asks the jury to believe a defendant who was not candid at the start. As the lawyers prepare their final arguments, Ishmael investigates the weather and maritime communications from the night Carl died.

The lawyers complete their arguments and the jury begins considering a case with no eyewitness to Carl's death. Ishmael, searching records at the lighthouse radio station, discovers that a freighter passed the island during the relevant period. Its wake reached the fishing grounds during a power failure, providing a coherent explanation for Carl's fatal head injury and fall: after Kabuo departed, Carl climbed his mast to deal with his lantern and was thrown by the unexpected swell. Ishmael takes the records but at first tells no one. Keeping silent could condemn Kabuo and preserve Ishmael's private hold on Hatsue's suffering. When Hatsue asks him to help, he finally rejects that impulse and gives her the evidence. Sheriff Moran verifies the new account, and the murder charge is dismissed before a verdict. Kabuo is reunited with his family. Hatsue does not return Ishmael's romantic hopes, but his decision breaks with years of self-pity and honors the journalistic integrity his father modeled. He records Carl's death as the accident the evidence shows it to have been.

characters.description: An elderly woman looking back on her life in nineteenth-century Hunan. As a girl from a modest farming family, Lily learns that the quality of her feet may give her an unusually favorable marriage. She is disciplined, eager to be worthy of love, and deeply shaped by the rules that confine women to domestic spaces and judge them through obedience, marriage, and sons.
characters.name: Lily

characters.description: The girl matched to Lily as her laotong, a formal lifelong counterpart meant to share an intimate bond deeper than ordinary friendship. Snow Flower appears refined and comes from a family believed to have higher standing than Lily's. Through messages written in nüshu, she gives Lily companionship and a private language for feelings their public lives do not permit.
characters.name: Snow Flower

characters.description: The matchmaker who recognizes that Lily's feet could transform her marriage prospects. Madame Wang arranges both Lily's laotong relationship with Snow Flower and the negotiations that will determine Lily's future household. She is worldly, authoritative, and one of the few women able to move regularly between otherwise separate families.
characters.name: Madame Wang

characters.description: Lily's mother, who prepares her daughters for the narrow duties expected of women. She supervises Lily's footbinding with severe resolve, believing that enduring pain and achieving the proper shape are necessary for her daughter's security and the family's advancement.
characters.name: Lily's mother

characters.description: Lily's cousin and childhood companion, close enough in age that they pass through footbinding and preparation for marriage together. Beautiful Moon shares the women's upstairs world with Lily and gives her an ordinary family friendship alongside the more formal bond with Snow Flower.
characters.name: Beautiful Moon

characters.description: Lily's younger sister, whose feet are bound with Lily's and Beautiful Moon's. Her body cannot withstand the infection that follows, showing Lily at an early age that the custom demanded as a condition of womanhood can also be fatal.
characters.name: Third Sister

characters.description: The man chosen as Lily's husband in the prosperous Lu family of Tongkou. At their marriage he is still largely a stranger to her, and their relationship is governed by family duty and the expectation that Lily will produce sons and serve his household.
characters.name: Lily's husband

characters.description: The senior woman in Lily's married household. Lady Lu evaluates the new bride according to her feet, manners, work, fertility, and obedience. Her approval carries immense weight as Lily learns the hierarchy of the wealthy family she has entered.
characters.name: Lady Lu

characters.description: Snow Flower's husband, a butcher whose trade places his family low in the local social order. His household is far poorer and harsher than the one Snow Flower's upbringing led Lily to expect, and his temper adds fear to the difficulties Snow Flower faces as a wife and mother.
characters.name: Snow Flower's husband

characters.description: Snow Flower's mother, once associated with a cultivated household but weakened by addiction and the family's decline. Her circumstances are part of the truth Snow Flower has been ashamed to tell Lily and help explain the difference between the girl's polished education and her actual marriage prospects.
characters.name: Snow Flower's mother

recaps.ending: After publicly condemning Snow Flower, Lily learns that she misunderstood her friend's message: Snow Flower's sworn sisters had offered companionship during suffering, not replaced the laotong bond. By then Snow Flower is gravely ill. Lily goes to her, nurses her through her final days, and hears how loneliness, abuse, poverty, and the deaths of her children shaped the choices Lily judged so harshly. Snow Flower dies with their attachment restored but without giving Lily the absolution she wants. Lily assumes responsibility for Snow Flower's surviving children and later hears further testimony from the women who had supported her. In old age, socially honored but burdened by remorse, Lily writes the history of their relationship and addresses Snow Flower's spirit. The fan preserves their nüshu messages, including evidence of Lily's failures as well as their love, and Lily asks forgiveness for having valued pride and social rules above a faithful understanding of her friend.
recaps.in_short: In nineteenth-century Hunan, Lily's carefully bound feet bring her a prestigious marriage and a formal laotong match with Snow Flower. The girls communicate in women's nüshu writing, especially on a fan, and promise lifelong devotion. Lily rises into a wealthy household, while Snow Flower reveals that her family has fallen and that she must marry an abusive butcher. Marriage, childbirth, poverty, and the Taiping upheaval widen the difference between their lives. During a dangerous mountain refuge, Snow Flower suffers another devastating loss. Later she writes of sworn sisters who comfort her; Lily reads this as rejection, publicly denounces her, and breaks their bond. She discovers too late that Snow Flower never meant to replace her. Lily nurses Snow Flower as she dies, cares for her children, and spends the rest of her life regretting that pride and convention made her fail the person she loved most.

recaps.text: From old age, Lily recalls growing up in a farming household in Hunan, where a girl's value is tied to marriage, obedience, and the sons she may bear. A visiting matchmaker, Madame Wang, decides Lily has feet capable of an exceptional result and recommends a binding schedule that may raise her above the marriage normally expected for her family. Lily, her cousin Beautiful Moon, and Third Sister begin the prolonged process together under the women's supervision. The pain is treated as necessary discipline. Third Sister develops a fatal infection, but Lily continues, driven by her mother's demands and the promise that success will secure her future. Madame Wang also proposes an unusual honor: Lily may be formally paired with a laotong, a girl of the same age whose matched qualities will make them lifelong counterparts.

Lily is matched with Snow Flower, a poised girl believed to come from a superior family. Their first message arrives on a fan in nüshu, the women's script used to exchange private thoughts within lives controlled by men and senior relatives. The girls visit, learn one another's habits, and promise a bond that will outlast marriage and physical separation. Snow Flower's polish introduces Lily to customs beyond her village, while Lily offers wholehearted loyalty. Through letters and shared festivals they grow emotionally inseparable. Madame Wang's prediction about Lily is also fulfilled: her bound feet and conduct secure a marriage into the wealthy Lu family in Tongkou. The match promises status but means that Lily must eventually leave her natal home and prove herself among strangers.

Lily enters the Lu household in the enclosed bridal chair and begins married life under Lady Lu's scrutiny. Her position improves as she meets domestic expectations and begins to bear children, especially sons. Snow Flower's situation proves painfully different from the image surrounding their match. Her family has declined, her mother is addicted to opium, and Snow Flower has been married to a butcher, a low-status trade associated with blood and death. Her husband is volatile and their household lives close to poverty. Lily feels deceived by the concealment but continues the laotong relationship. Their meetings and messages now cross an increasing social distance: Lily is becoming an honored wife, while Snow Flower faces hunger, fear, and repeated uncertainty about her children's survival.

The women's adult lives are defined by pregnancies, births, illness, and the demands of their husbands' families. Lily's production of sons strengthens her authority in the Lu household. Snow Flower loses children and endures her husband's anger, yet she often minimizes her suffering when writing to Lily. The Taiping conflict then drives both families from their homes. They shelter in the mountains through brutal winter conditions with little food or protection. Social distinctions offer limited defense against cold, violence, and disease. Snow Flower suffers another devastating loss, and Lily struggles to respond with the tenderness their old promises require. Although they survive and return from the mountains, grief and the unequal shape of their lives have placed strain inside a bond both women once believed unbreakable.

Now an influential woman in her community, Lily increasingly applies the standards of her prosperous household to Snow Flower's choices. When Snow Flower writes that a group of sworn sisters has comforted her, Lily interprets the message as a declaration that their exclusive laotong bond has been discarded. Hurt pride turns into punishment. Lily composes a formal condemnation and repeats her grievances publicly, exposing Snow Flower's private failures and isolating her further. Only afterward does Lily learn that the sworn sisters supplemented rather than replaced Snow Flower's devotion and that they were present when Lily was not. Snow Flower becomes gravely ill. Confronted with the damage caused by her certainty, Lily returns to her former companion, but illness has made time for repair very short.

Lily nurses Snow Flower and listens as the hidden extent of her friend's suffering becomes clear. Snow Flower dies after the two acknowledge their enduring love, leaving Lily reconciled but unable to undo her public betrayal. Lily takes responsibility for Snow Flower's surviving children and speaks with the sworn sisters, who explain how faithfully Snow Flower continued to think of her. Decades later, Lily has achieved the position once promised by her excellent feet: she is a respected elder surrounded by descendants. That success cannot erase her remorse. She records the women's story in nüshu and preserves the fan that carried their messages across childhood, marriage, war, estrangement, and death. Addressing Snow Flower beyond the grave, Lily asks forgiveness and recognizes that rigid ideas of duty kept her from fully hearing the person to whom she had pledged her life.

aliases: His Grace, the Duke of Ankh
characters.description: Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and, by marriage, Duke of Ankh, a rank he has never become reconciled to. A copper by instinct and conviction, suspicious of privilege, including his own, and grimly aware of how much anger he keeps under control. He is a devoted, awkward father who reads his small son a bedtime story every night without fail, and he is about to be removed from the city and the job for the first time in his adult life.
characters.name: Sam Vimes

characters.description: The Patrician of Ankh-Morpork, who governs by knowing exactly what people will do and arranging matters accordingly. He has taken an interest in the idea of Commander Vimes being sent somewhere with no crime in it.
characters.name: Lord Vetinari

characters.description: Vimes's wife: an aristocrat by birth, a dragon breeder by enthusiasm, and immovable once she has decided what is good for her family. She has inherited a large country estate and has determined that her husband is going to take a holiday on it.
characters.name: Lady Sybil

characters.description: Vimes's six-year-old son, cheerful, observant, and currently engrossed in a natural history of animal droppings, a subject he can discuss at any length and in any company.
characters.name: Young Sam

characters.description: The Vimes household's gentleman's gentleman: impeccably correct, quietly amused, and equipped with a past on the streets that he has never entirely put down. He carries useful things in his hat and is a great deal more dangerous than any butler needs to be.
characters.name: Willikins

characters.description: The landlord of the village pub, an incomer with a professional welcome and a very good memory for faces, who recognizes Vimes rather faster than a country publican should. He knows a good deal about what happens locally and is careful about which parts of it he mentions.
characters.name: Jiminy

characters.description: A retired officer among the local gentry, straight-backed, courteous, and rather more troubled by the district's arrangements than his neighbours are. He has old-fashioned ideas about honour that his acquaintances find inconvenient.
characters.name: Colonel Makepeace

characters.description: The young local chief constable, the third generation of his family to hold the post, with no training, no colleagues, and a rule book he has largely worked out for himself. Earnest, badly out of his depth, and braver than his situation deserves.
characters.name: Feeney Upshot

characters.description: A goblin who attaches himself to Vimes: filthy, evil-smelling, sardonic, and entirely unbothered by either fact. He knows the country, the caves, and the river better than anyone alive, and turns up whenever Vimes is about to need him.
characters.name: Stinky

characters.description: A writer of children's books who lives locally and is regarded by the county as an eccentric. She has spent years among the goblins, has learned their language and their beliefs, and teaches those who will learn, which the neighbourhood considers at best foolish.
characters.name: Miss Felicity Beedle

characters.description: A young goblin woman living in the caves above the estate, taught music by Miss Beedle, who plays the harp with a skill that is impossible to explain away. What she can do is an argument in itself about what goblins are.
characters.name: Tears of the Mushroom

characters.description: A local man who works as an enforcer for people with money: fast, capable, and entirely without hesitation, and unusual even among killers in that he seems to feel nothing about it at all.
characters.name: Stratford

characters.description: A veteran Ankh-Morpork Watch sergeant of limited ambition and considerable seniority, who handles an item of goblin property in the course of a routine inquiry and begins, slowly and frighteningly, to stop being himself.
characters.name: Sergeant Colon

characters.description: A six-inch-tall Watch officer who was raised by gnomes and does the jobs no full-sized copper can, going into places nobody thinks to guard. He is a formidable fighter and is beginning to have questions about where he actually came from.
characters.name: Wee Mad Arthur

recaps.ending: Vimes proves the case: local landowners, with money and a name behind them, have been shipping goblins abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations and running smuggled goods on the same boats, and a young goblin woman was murdered to keep it quiet. Stratford, the killer, makes a last attempt on Vimes and on his family, and is taken; the aristocrat who financed the trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that leave him with nothing. The captured goblins are freed, Sergeant Colon recovers once the goblin pot he was carrying is returned to its owners, and the young country constable Feeney Upshot finishes the case as a real policeman with a future in the Watch. The decisive stroke is not an arrest: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork's Opera House, in front of the city's wealthy and powerful, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp, and an audience that had always been told goblins were vermin sits and listens to one make music. On the strength of that, and of the case Vimes has built, the law changes and goblins become people, with the rights that follow. Vimes goes home to the city and the job, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, as everyone including his wife expected, into police work.
recaps.in_short: Sam Vimes, Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and reluctant Duke of Ankh, is made to take a holiday at his wife's country estate, where he finds that a copper is still a copper. The district's goblins are treated as vermin, which under local law they are, and a young goblin woman has been murdered. The local chief constable, a young man named Feeney Upshot, arrests Vimes for it; Vimes turns him into a deputy instead, and together they uncover a trade run by the county's own gentry, shipping goblins abroad as slaves and smuggling goods on the return leg, with a professional killer named Stratford enforcing it. Vimes pursues the boats downriver through a flood, is nearly killed, and brings the evidence and the survivors back. The case ends not only in arrests but in a change of the law: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork a goblin girl plays the harp for the city's rich and powerful, and goblins are recognized as people. Vimes returns to the city with his family, his holiday having gone exactly as everyone expected.

recaps.text: Previously, in earlier books: Sam Vimes rose from a drunken night watchman to Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch, rebuilding it into a large mixed force of humans, dwarfs, trolls, werewolves, and others, and became Duke of Ankh through his marriage to the aristocratic Lady Sybil Ramkin, a title he has never enjoyed. He answers, grudgingly, to Lord Vetinari, the Patrician, who finds him useful precisely because he cannot be bought or flattered. Vimes distrusts privilege, especially his own, polices by the principle that the law applies to everybody or it is not the law, and keeps a tight hold on his own temper because he knows what is underneath it. During an earlier case an ancient dwarfish thing got into his head and has remained there since, watching, as a kind of unwelcome guardian. He and Sybil have a young son, and Vimes's fiercest personal rule is that he is home to read to the boy at six o'clock.

Vimes is manoeuvred by his wife, with Lord Vetinari's approval, into taking the first holiday of his adult life: a stay at the Ramkin family's country estate, along with Lady Sybil, six-year-old Young Sam, and Willikins. The countryside receives him as a duke, which he loathes, and he discovers immediately that he does not know how to stop being a policeman. He notices the things the locals no longer see: the careful way people talk around certain subjects, the deference that goes slightly wrong, and the goblins who live in the hills above the estate and are regarded by everybody as vermin, which under the law here is exactly what they are.

Vimes explores the village and its pub, where the landlord recognizes him faster than any country publican should. He meets the local gentry at dinner and finds them polite, incurious, and united in the view that goblins are pests to be cleared. Young Sam, meanwhile, has fallen in love with a local children's author's book about animal droppings and pursues the subject relentlessly. Vimes takes note of a young local man who talks to him about the goblins and then is not seen again, and of the fact that nobody appears to consider this worth reporting. The country grows quietly more hostile the longer he asks questions, and the smell of a crime he cannot yet name settles over the whole estate.

Vimes finds the body of a young goblin woman who has been beaten to death. Under local law this is not murder, because a goblin is not a person, and the district has no intention of treating it as one. Feeney Upshot, the young and entirely untrained chief constable, arrives and arrests Vimes for the killing; Vimes, who could have stopped him, allows it, then takes charge of both the arrest and the constable, and begins turning him into a real policeman. Back in Ankh-Morpork the Watch has picked up a goblin item as evidence, and Sergeant Colon, who has handled it, is being slowly and frighteningly taken over by whatever is bound up in it. Vimes starts building a case in a place where the local magistrates, the local money, and the local law are all on the other side.

Vimes goes up into the goblin caves and learns what the district has been careful not to know: the goblins have a religion, a language, a craft, and a rigorous moral code, and one young goblin woman, taught by the local children's author, plays the harp well enough to settle the question of what goblins are for anyone honest enough to listen. The reason for the murder becomes clear as the trade behind it surfaces: goblins have been rounded up and shipped abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations, with smuggled goods carried on the return trips, organized and financed by people with land, titles, and friends. Enforcing it is Stratford, a local killer who works without hesitation or feeling, and who now knows that the Duke of Ankh is asking questions.

With Feeney beside him and a goblin guide who knows every inch of the country, Vimes goes after the boats carrying the captured goblins downriver. A storm turns into a flood, and the pursuit becomes a night run down a rising river that no sane person would attempt, ending with Vimes half drowned and washed up a long way from anywhere. In the city, Wee Mad Arthur works the docks and the warehouses from angles nobody thinks to guard, following the smuggled goods back to the people paying for them, and turns up an unexpected fact about his own origins along the way. Vimes survives, catches up with the boats, and takes them, and the surviving goblins are freed and, for the first time, in the hands of somebody prepared to treat what was done to them as a crime.

The pursuit ends downriver at Quirm, where Vimes, filthy and exhausted, hands over prisoners, evidence, and a case, and is put back together by the local Watch and eventually by his wife. Stratford, however, is not among those taken, and is loose and moving. Vimes returns to the estate and then to Ankh-Morpork with everything he needs: witnesses, documents, the boats, and the survivors. Sergeant Colon is freed of what he was carrying once the goblin property is returned to the people it belongs to. Feeney, having done everything asked of him and rather more, is no longer a village constable in anything but title, and the question is no longer whether the crime can be proved but whether a court will accept that a crime against goblins is a crime at all.

The case moves to the city, where the law, not the arrests, is the real battleground: everything Vimes has depends on goblins being people, and at present they legally are not. Vetinari, who has been several steps ahead throughout, arranges the occasion for settling it, a concert at the Opera House before an audience of the city's wealthiest and most influential. Vimes prepares the evidence, Miss Beedle prepares her pupil, and the aristocratic families behind the trade prepare to brazen it out. Stratford, who has nothing left to lose, makes his own preparations, and they involve Vimes's household.

At the Opera House, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp in front of the city's rich and powerful, and an audience raised to believe goblins were vermin listens to one make music. That, together with the case Vimes has built, is enough: the law is changed and goblins become people, with everything that follows from it. Stratford makes his last attempt, going after Vimes and his family, and is taken; the estate is set alight in the course of it. The aristocrat who financed the slaving trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that strip him of everything, the freed goblins are given standing and protection, Sergeant Colon recovers, and Feeney Upshot ends the affair as a genuine policeman with a career in front of him. Vimes goes home to Ankh-Morpork with his wife and son, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, exactly as everyone expected, into police work.

characters.description: A drow who has left the Underdark entirely and climbed to the surface world, having renounced his people, his family and their goddess. He is a superb fighter with two scimitars, but on the surface almost every advantage he has is gone: daylight blinds and burns him, he cannot read the weather or the seasons, and his appearance guarantees that anyone who sees him will assume the worst. What he wants is not safety but a place where he can be judged by what he does.
characters.name: Drizzt Do'Urden

characters.description: A great black panther summoned from another world by an onyx figurine Drizzt carries, able to remain for a limited time before she must return and rest. She is Drizzt's oldest friend and, in the first surface years, his only one.
characters.name: Guenhwyvar

characters.description: A human farming family working land near the village of Maldobar on the northern frontier: parents, grandfather and several children, ordinary and unguarded. Drizzt watches them from the treeline for weeks, drawn by the domestic life he has never had and certain that showing himself would only terrify them.
characters.name: The Thistledown Family

characters.description: A barghest, a predatory creature from another plane growing toward its full power in a lair above the valley. It gains strength by killing, wears a monstrous shape, and treats the human settlements below as a larder rather than a threat.
characters.name: Ulgulu

characters.description: Ulgulu's brother and fellow barghest, junior in the pairing and impatient with it. He shares the lair, the servants and the appetite.
characters.name: Kempfana

characters.description: A quickling in the barghests' service, a tiny sprite who moves and speaks so fast that his words run together into a single stream. He scouts, carries messages and takes a malicious pleasure in arranging trouble for others.
characters.name: Tephanis

characters.description: A frontier bounty hunter, large, loud and well known in the region, who tracks men for money with the help of a trained dog. He is not fussy about evidence, and once he has settled on a quarry no correction reaches him.
characters.name: Roddy McGristle

characters.description: A surface elf archer of the northern woods who joins the hunt for the dark elf. Unlike the humans on the trail he actually studies the tracks and the pattern of what his quarry does and does not do, and what he finds does not match the crime he was told about.
characters.name: Kellindil

characters.description: An old human ranger, blind for years, who lives alone in a fortified grove high in the mountains and keeps watch on the orc tribes below. He navigates by hearing, memory and the animals who live with him, fights well enough to embarrass men half his age, and judges people entirely by conduct. He follows the goddess Mielikki and has been waiting a long time for someone worth teaching.
characters.name: Montolio DeBrouchee

characters.description: An owl who lives in Montolio's grove and serves as one of the old ranger's eyes, carrying scouting reports back to him in a language the two of them have worked out between them.
characters.name: Hooter

characters.description: The chieftain of the orc tribes of the mountains below Montolio's grove, held in check for years by the old ranger's watchfulness and looking for any excuse or ally that would let him move.
characters.name: Graul

characters.description: Drizzt's surviving brother and the chief warrior of House Do'Urden, sent up out of the Underdark with a hunting party to finish the family's long-standing business. He has no interest in the surface beyond the errand.
characters.name: Dinin Do'Urden

characters.description: Drizzt's sister, the priestess who raised him, now the surviving religious authority of a ruined house. Restoring House Do'Urden means delivering Drizzt to the Spider Queen, and she is the one who insists the hunt continue onto the surface.
characters.name: Vierna Do'Urden

characters.description: A dwarf king in Icewind Dale, leader of a clan that mines the valley beneath Kelvin's Cairn near the ten frontier towns. Gruff, blunt and entirely unimpressed by reputations, he takes people at the value of their work and is stubborn enough to argue a whole region into changing its mind.
characters.name: Bruenor Battlehammer

characters.description: A human girl orphaned in a raid and raised by Bruenor as his own daughter among the dwarves. Still a child, curious and without any of the frontier's inherited fears, she is the first person in Icewind Dale to treat the dark elf as simply another neighbor.
characters.name: Catti-brie

recaps.ending: The attack on Montolio's grove costs Drizzt the first home he has had on the surface. The orcs are broken and the drow hunting party is driven back underground, but Montolio is killed in the fighting. Drizzt buries the old ranger, keeps Hooter and the grove's animals in mind as he goes, and holds to the ranger's code and the goddess Mielikki that Montolio gave him rather than sliding back into the hunter he was in the Underdark. Kellindil and the elves of the region, who watched what Drizzt actually did rather than what he was, no longer count him an enemy. Because no settled place will have him and because staying anywhere populated invites the next hunt, Drizzt goes north to Icewind Dale, a frozen frontier at the edge of the maps where people are judged mainly on whether they are useful in a fight. The ten towns there greet him with the usual fear, but the dwarf king Bruenor Battlehammer takes his own measure of him, speaks for him, and offers him a place in the dwarven valley beneath Kelvin's Cairn; Bruenor's adopted human daughter Catti-brie befriends him outright. Drizzt's exile ends not with the world's acceptance but with a handful of people willing to take him as he is.
recaps.in_short: Drizzt Do'Urden climbs out of the Underdark into a surface world that blinds him, and spends his first years there learning to live under a sky and watching human farms from a distance because he knows his face will terrify anyone who sees it. When the barghest Ulgulu slaughters a farming family he has been quietly watching, the drow tracks nearby make Drizzt the obvious culprit, and the bounty hunter Roddy McGristle takes up a pursuit that outlasts every fact against it. Drizzt destroys the real killers, cannot clear his name, and retreats into the mountains for years. There he finds Montolio DeBrouchee, an old blind ranger who takes him in, teaches him the surface world, names what he already is, and introduces him to the goddess Mielikki. It is the first home he has had. When a drow hunting party led by his brother comes up after him and the local orcs are turned loose on the grove, the attack is beaten off but Montolio is killed. Drizzt travels north to Icewind Dale, where the dwarf king Bruenor Battlehammer speaks for him and offers him a home.

recaps.text: Previously: Drizzt Do'Urden was born into a noble house of the drow city Menzoberranzan and raised to serve the Spider Queen, whose cruelty he could never make himself accept. Trained into a superb swordsman by the house weapon master Zaknafein, he broke with his people after a raid on the surface in which he refused to kill an elf child, renounced the goddess, and fled his family for the wild tunnels of the Underdark. His desertion cost the house the goddess's favor, and his mother sacrificed Zaknafein, who was in fact his father, in his place. Drizzt survived ten years alone in the tunnels with only the summoned panther Guenhwyvar for company, nearly losing himself to the instinctive killing state that kept him alive. He found shelter for a time among the deep gnomes of Blingdenstone and made friends there, but his family's hunt followed him and killed one of them. Rather than let the gnomes pay any more on his account, he refused their offer of a home and set out for the surface world he had seen only once, on the raid that broke his faith.

Drizzt reaches the surface and finds it almost unlivable. Daylight blinds and burns him, so he sleeps in caves along the mountains and moves only at night, teaching himself weather, seasons and the behavior of animals from scratch. Hunger and loneliness push him toward the settled valleys, where he watches human farms from the treeline: he wants company badly enough to take the risk of being seen, and knows well enough what being seen would mean. Above the same valley, in a lair worked into the rock, the barghest brothers Ulgulu and Kempfana feed on travellers and livestock to grow toward their full power, served by the quickling Tephanis and a rabble of goblins.

Drizzt spends weeks watching the Thistledown farm near the village of Maldobar, close enough that the children catch glimpses of him. Ulgulu, hunting, kills the family. Drow tracks around the farm and a frightened village make Drizzt the obvious murderer, and the frontier turns out to hunt him. The bounty hunter Roddy McGristle leads the search; in the fighting Drizzt is forced to kill Roddy's dog and leaves Roddy with a permanent facial wound and a grudge that will outlast every fact. Drizzt tracks the real killers to their lair and destroys Ulgulu and Kempfana, but there is no one he can tell, and no one who would believe a dark elf if he did.

Unable to clear his name, Drizzt goes north into the high country and lives alone again for years, deliberately avoiding people. Roddy McGristle keeps hunting him; his obsession costs him his standing with the local authorities and does not slow him down. Elves of the region take up the trail as well, among them the archer Kellindil, who studies the tracks and the pattern of the killings closely enough to notice that the evidence and the accusation do not fit together. Drizzt, meanwhile, has begun to slide back toward the wordless hunter he was underground, with nothing on the surface to hold him to anything else.

High in the mountains Drizzt finds a fortified grove kept by Montolio DeBrouchee, an old blind ranger who lives among animals, watches the orc tribes below, and judges by conduct because he cannot judge by sight. Montolio takes him in. Over a long winter he teaches Drizzt the surface world in earnest: woodcraft, weather, the names of things, how to fight beside allies rather than alone. He tells Drizzt that what he has been doing by instinct has a name, ranger, and introduces him to the goddess Mielikki, whom Drizzt accepts. For the first time since he left Menzoberranzan, Drizzt has a friend, a purpose and a place. Below the grove the orc chieftain Graul gathers his tribes, and word that a rogue drow is living on the surface makes its way back down to Menzoberranzan.

House Do'Urden, ruined and desperate to recover the Spider Queen's favor, sends a hunting party up to the surface under Drizzt's brother Dinin, at his sister Vierna's insistence. Roddy McGristle is still on the trail as well. Graul's orcs are set loose on Montolio's grove, and the grove's defenders fight a running battle through the trees and the prepared ground the old ranger has spent years laying out. Drizzt and Guenhwyvar break the assault and drive the drow party back toward the tunnels, but the victory is expensive: Montolio is killed. Drizzt buries him and keeps the promise implied in everything the old man taught him.

With the grove empty and no settled community willing to have him, Drizzt heads north to Icewind Dale, a frozen frontier at the edge of the known lands where ten small towns scrape a living from the tundra and the lake fishing. He is met there with the reaction he expects, but the dwarf king Bruenor Battlehammer, whose clan mines the valley beneath Kelvin's Cairn, judges him by what he does rather than what he is, speaks for him publicly, and offers him a cave on the mountain and the dwarves' company when he wants it. Bruenor's adopted human daughter Catti-brie, still a child, befriends him without hesitation. Drizzt's long journey out of the Underdark ends here: not with a world that accepts him, but with a place he can stay and a few people who will vouch for him.

characters.description: A conscientious New York lawyer whose thirtieth birthday prompts an uncomfortable review of the cautious choices she has made. She has spent much of her life accommodating her charismatic best friend Darcy, even when doing so has meant suppressing her own wishes.
characters.name: Rachel White

characters.description: Rachel's lifelong best friend and Dex's fiancée. Beautiful, socially confident, and accustomed to being the center of their shared circle, she organizes Rachel's birthday celebration while looking forward to her own approaching wedding.
characters.name: Darcy Rhone

characters.description: Darcy's fiancé and Rachel's former law-school classmate. Rachel introduced him to Darcy despite having feelings for him herself, and he is now weeks away from marrying her best friend.
characters.name: Dexter Thaler

characters.description: Rachel and Darcy's close friend, now living in London. Direct and perceptive, he knows the history of their friendship and becomes the confidant to whom Rachel can admit what she is hiding from everyone in New York.
characters.name: Ethan

characters.description: Rachel's frank colleague and friend. Less invested in Darcy's charm than the rest of the social circle, she offers Rachel a judgment that is loyal to Rachel rather than to the appearance of harmony.
characters.name: Hillary

characters.description: Dex's single friend, whose easygoing manner makes him a plausible date for Rachel during the group's summer weekends. He avoids commitment and generally treats romance more casually than Rachel does.
characters.name: Marcus

characters.description: A friend in Rachel and Darcy's New York circle who is openly interested in Ethan. Her questions and expectations make Rachel's attempts to conceal the truth within the group more complicated.
characters.name: Claire

characters.description: A childhood friend of Rachel and Darcy in Indiana. Her settled married life gives Rachel another perspective on the rivalry and compromises that have shaped the old friendship.
characters.name: Annalise

recaps.ending: Dex finally ends his engagement and goes to Rachel, choosing their relationship rather than proceeding with the wedding. Before Rachel and Dex can decide how to tell Darcy, Darcy arrives and confesses that she has also been unfaithful: she has been sleeping with Marcus and is pregnant by him. The disclosure initially seems to release Rachel from her guilt, but Darcy discovers that Dex is in Rachel's apartment and realizes the affair has involved her fiancé and her oldest friend. The confrontation ends Rachel and Darcy's friendship, and the wedding is canceled. Rachel and Dex remain together, now without secrecy but aware of the hurt surrounding their beginning. Darcy's plan to build a future with Marcus does not hold. Later, visibly pregnant and preparing to leave for London, she encounters Rachel. Their exchange is restrained rather than reconciliatory. Rachel closes the story having made a choice for herself, while accepting that gaining Dex has cost her the friendship that defined much of her earlier life.
recaps.in_short: At her thirtieth birthday, cautious lawyer Rachel White sleeps with Dex Thaler, the fiancé of her lifelong best friend Darcy Rhone. Rachel has loved Dex since law school but introduced him to Darcy and habitually yielded to her more forceful friend. What seems like one betrayal becomes a continuing affair after Dex admits that he shares Rachel's feelings. Through a summer of group weekends, Rachel and Dex meet secretly while Darcy plans the wedding and Rachel uses dates with Dex's friend Marcus as cover. Confidants Ethan and Hillary push Rachel to stop accepting indefinite promises, and she demands that Dex choose. He eventually leaves Darcy and comes to Rachel. Darcy then reveals that she has been sleeping with Marcus and is pregnant, only to discover Dex in Rachel's apartment and understand their affair. The wedding and the women's friendship end. Rachel and Dex stay together; Darcy's relationship with Marcus fails, and she prepares to leave for London without reconciling with Rachel.

recaps.text: New York lawyer Rachel White turns thirty at a party organized by her lifelong best friend, Darcy Rhone. Rachel has long been the cautious counterpart to Darcy's confidence and has often let Darcy take the more desirable role in their friendship. That history includes Dex Thaler, Rachel's law-school friend: Rachel was attracted to him but introduced him to Darcy, and he is now Darcy's fiancé. After Darcy leaves the birthday celebration, Rachel and Dex continue drinking, share a taxi, and sleep together. The next morning Rachel is ashamed and expects them to treat the night as an isolated mistake. Instead, the encounter forces her to admit that her feelings for Dex never disappeared and that her loyalty to Darcy is entangled with years of resentment.

Rachel and Dex speak again and acknowledge that the birthday night was not emotionally meaningless. Dex says that he has feelings for Rachel and doubts his coming marriage, but he does not immediately end the engagement. Their contact becomes an affair conducted around Darcy's wedding plans and the assumptions of their shared friends. Rachel confides in Ethan, an old friend living in London who understands the unequal pattern between Rachel and Darcy and refuses to let Rachel describe herself only as a passive participant. Rachel's colleague Hillary also becomes an ally. Both recognize that Dex's uncertainty leaves Rachel carrying secrecy and guilt while he retains his public future with Darcy.

The friends begin their summer routine, including weekends away together, which puts Rachel beside Darcy and Dex while the affair continues. Rachel dates Dex's friend Marcus, partly as camouflage and partly in an effort to test a simpler alternative, but Marcus is casual and does not offer the bond she wants. Dex finds private time with Rachel and continues to say that his relationship with Darcy is wrong, yet the wedding remains scheduled. Darcy talks freely about the ceremony and her future, unaware that her best friend and fiancé are withholding the central fact of their lives. The strain makes Rachel reconsider memories in which Darcy competed with her or claimed her opportunities, though those grievances do not erase Rachel's responsibility for the present betrayal.

Rachel's secrecy spreads into the rest of the social circle as she tries to explain absences, meetings, and her apparent romantic situation without exposing Dex. Claire's interest in Ethan adds pressure to the cover stories, while Ethan and Hillary continue to tell Rachel that waiting indefinitely is not a decision. A visit to Indiana and contact with childhood friend Annalise remind Rachel how long Darcy has defined the terms of their friendship. Rachel also sees that she has used Darcy's selfishness to justify avoiding a direct choice of her own. Dex remains divided between the expectations around his engagement and the relationship he says he wants with Rachel, leaving the two women to plan incompatible futures around him.

As the wedding approaches, Rachel can no longer accept Dex's assurances without action. She requires him to choose and prepares herself for the likelihood that he will marry Darcy. The affair stops feeling like a private exception and becomes a decision about the life each of them will publicly live. Rachel considers the loss of Darcy, the judgment of their friends, and the possibility that Dex's hesitation reveals a permanent weakness. Dex at last breaks the engagement and comes to Rachel, showing that he has chosen her. They are together in Rachel's apartment but have not yet managed the disclosure to Darcy or the consequences for the wider group.

Darcy unexpectedly arrives at Rachel's apartment with a confession of her own: she has been sleeping with Marcus and is pregnant by him. She expects the news to explain the end of her engagement, but then discovers Dex with Rachel and realizes that their relationship has been continuing behind her back. The symmetry does not produce forgiveness. Darcy sees the affair as a betrayal by the two people closest to her, and her friendship with Rachel ends in anger. The wedding is canceled, while Rachel and Dex remain together and begin a relationship that no longer depends on secrecy. Darcy's intended future with Marcus soon falls apart. Later Rachel encounters her visibly pregnant former friend as Darcy prepares to leave for London. They do not reconcile, but the meeting is less explosive than their confrontation. Rachel accepts both her chosen life with Dex and the lasting cost of ending the old pattern with Darcy.

characters.description: A gentle, determined girl in the same rigidly controlled community from the start of the series, assigned the role of Birthmother, or Vessel, to produce infants for the society. She is only fourteen when she bears her first child. Unlike others around her, she is not fully numbed to feeling, and she forms a fierce, forbidden attachment to the son she was never meant to know. That love becomes the driving purpose of her life.
characters.name: Claire

characters.description: Claire's infant son, the baby she bears in the controlled community and is forbidden to keep. In that society children are assigned to family units, and this small, restless infant does not thrive on its rigid schedule. He is the child at the center of Claire's search, and the thread that ties her story to the wider world of the series.
characters.name: Gabe

characters.description: A young man, known from earlier in the series, who once fled the controlled community as a boy carrying an infant to safety and later became the wise leader of a welcoming settlement. He is marked by pale eyes and a gift for perception. Claire's search will eventually cross paths with the community he guides.
characters.name: Jonas

characters.description: A young man in a remote, isolated settlement, patient and kind, who helps Claire rebuild her strength and teaches her the difficult skill of climbing the steep cliff that walls the village off from the world beyond. He bears the marks of a hard past of his own and understands, better than most, the danger of wanting something badly enough to pay any price for it.
characters.name: Einar

characters.description: A smooth, sinister figure who offers people the thing they most desire in exchange for something of themselves, always at a hidden and ruinous cost. He deals in longing and weakness, and his bargains bind those who accept them. He is the shadow that has moved through the wider world of the series, and he stands between Claire and what she seeks.
characters.name: Trademaster

characters.description: A young woman known from earlier in the series, born with a twisted leg and gifted at weaving, who once uncovered the lies of her harsh home village and chose to work for change. She is now part of the wider community of settlements where much of the later story unfolds.
characters.name: Kira

recaps.ending: Claire's long search ends at the community led by the pale-eyed young man from the start of the series, where her son Gabe has grown into a teenager, ignorant that his mother is the frail, prematurely aged woman who has arrived among them. Her age is the price she paid the Trademaster to complete her journey. Gabe comes to understand who she is and discovers that he possesses a rare gift of his own, the ability to send his mind into another person. He seeks out the Trademaster and confronts him directly. Rather than fighting with force, Gabe uses his gift to make the Trademaster confront his own name and the hollow, joyless nature of what he is, and this recognition destroys him. With the villain undone, the bargain that stole Claire's youth is broken and she is made whole and young again. Mother and son are reunited, and the quartet closes on the linked communities at peace, the long harm of the controlled society and the Trademaster's cruelty finally answered.
recaps.in_short: Claire is a fourteen-year-old Birthmother in the rigidly controlled community of the series' opening, who bears a son through a difficult surgery and is quietly reassigned to other work. Unnumbed to feeling, she becomes fixated on the boy, Gabe, and when the infant is spirited out of the community to save his life, she is separated from him by a disaster at sea. Washed ashore with no memory in a remote cliffbound village, she slowly recovers, and once she learns she is a mother searching for her child, she trains for years to climb out and follow him. To complete her journey she strikes a bargain with the sinister Trademaster, trading away her youth, and arrives aged and weakened at the welcoming settlement where Gabe, now a young man, has grown up under the wise Leader. Gabe discovers his own gift for entering others' minds, confronts Trademaster, and destroys him by forcing him to face his own emptiness. With the villain undone, the bargain is broken, Claire is restored, and mother and son are reunited at last.

recaps.text: Earlier in the series: A boy named Jonas, chosen to hold his controlled community's suppressed memories, learned the truth about its comforts and cruelties and fled with an infant to save the baby's life, reaching a gentler world. In a separate harsh village, an orphaned girl named Kira, gifted at weaving, exposed her rulers' lies and stayed to work for change. In a welcoming community called Village, a young messenger named Matty, who could pass through the surrounding Forest, gave his life to heal the land when the community's hearts hardened and the Forest turned deadly; Jonas now leads that world of linked settlements. This story returns to the beginning, to the controlled community, and to the mother of the infant Jonas once carried to safety.

In the rigidly ordered community of the series' opening, a girl named Claire has been assigned the role of Birthmother, producing infants for a society that assigns children to family units and dulls its people to strong feeling. At only fourteen she bears a son through a difficult birth that requires surgery, and afterward she is quietly reassigned to different work. Because the process left her without the usual numbing routine, Claire is not as deadened as those around her, and she finds herself drawn with dangerous intensity toward the child she was never meant to know or keep. That secret, forbidden love begins to shape everything she will do.

aliases: the Wicked Witch of the West
characters.description: The green-skinned woman Oz remembers as the Wicked Witch of the West, dead before this book begins. She spent her last years shut up in the mountain castle of Kiamo Ko, and she died there when a girl from another world threw water on her. She never acknowledged Liir as her son and never denied it either. Her cloak, her broom, her reputation and her enemies are all he has to start from.
characters.name: Elphaba

characters.description: A young man of about fifteen, raised in the mountain fastness of Kiamo Ko in the household of the woman Oz calls the Wicked Witch of the West. Nobody will tell him plainly whether she was his mother, and he has no idea who his father might be; the question shapes everything he does. Uncertain, easily overlooked, and painfully aware that he has no standing anywhere, he leaves the castle after her death carrying her cloak and her broom, with no plan beyond finding the one person from that household he still hopes is alive. The novel alternates between his years of drifting through a changing Oz and a later moment when he is carried, broken and unconscious, into a rural convent.
characters.name: Liir

characters.description: A young Quadling woman newly delivered to the Cloister of Saint Glinda, set apart from the other maunts by her silence: she has almost no Ozish and does not speak to those around her. She plays a stringed instrument called a domingon, and she is set to sit with the dying stranger in the infirmary on the theory that music may reach him where medicine cannot. She is said to have a gift for sensing the present moment, rather than the past or the future.
characters.name: Candle

characters.description: The elderly head of the Cloister of Saint Glinda, a rural convent that takes in the sick, the unwanted and the inconvenient. Practical, dry and unsentimental after decades of governing difficult women, she decides how the house will treat its anonymous, half-dead guest, and she asks considerably fewer questions about him than her infirmarians would like.
characters.name: The Superior Maunt

characters.description: A Munchkinlander maunt who compounds the cloister's medicines. Curious, talkative and quick to theorize, she takes charge of the broken stranger's care alongside Sister Doctor, with whom she argues about everything from his injuries to his origins.
characters.name: Sister Apothecaire

characters.description: The cloister's physician, a maunt of considerable self-regard who considers herself the house's authority on anything clinical. She works with, and constantly against, Sister Apothecaire over the unconscious patient in the infirmary.
characters.name: Sister Doctor

characters.description: An impossibly old woman living out her last years among the maunts, nearly blind and generally treated by the house as a harmless lunatic. She takes an unsettling interest in the stranger in the infirmary and speaks as though she has been waiting for him, hinting at a knowledge of the dead Witch's family that she will not explain.
characters.name: Yackle

characters.description: The daughter of the Vinkus prince Fiyero and his wife Sarima, and Liir's childhood companion at Kiamo Ko. Years before this book opens, soldiers of the Emerald City carried off the women and children of that household. Nor is the one person from it Liir believes may still be living, and finding her is the errand that sends him out into Oz.
characters.name: Nor

characters.description: A blunt, well-meaning girl from another world who arrives at Kiamo Ko with three companions and leaves it with the Witch dead behind her. She is baffled rather than triumphant about what has happened, and she lets Liir attach himself to her party for the journey east to the Emerald City.
characters.name: Dorothy

characters.description: The ancient nurse who served the Witch's family for three generations and is left rattling around Kiamo Ko once the household collapses. Her memory drifts, and what she can be persuaded to say about Liir's origins is by turns tantalizing and useless.
characters.name: Nanny

characters.description: The most articulate of the winged monkeys the Witch kept at Kiamo Ko, taught to speak after a fashion and left behind with the rest of the castle's household. He is fonder of Liir than anyone else in Oz is.
characters.name: Chistery

characters.description: The princess of the Scrow, a nomadic people of the western grasslands, who is in truth an Elephant held by an old spell in human shape. Age is wearing the disguise thin and she can neither keep it nor shed it. Meeting Liir on the road, she recognizes what he is connected to and asks him, when the time comes, to help her die as herself.
characters.name: Princess Nastoya

characters.description: The dead Witch's younger brother, a charming and unscrupulous operator who moves in and out of the prison beneath the Emerald City as though he owned it, trading favors, contraband and information. He is the nearest thing to family Liir meets in the city, and he is helpful exactly as far as it suits him.
characters.name: Shell

characters.description: The straw man who walked to the Emerald City with Dorothy and is installed on the throne after the Wizard's departure, an arrangement that convinces nobody for long. Whether the figure sitting on the throne is even the same one who made that journey is a question people in the city have learned not to ask aloud.
characters.name: The Scarecrow

characters.description: A capable, courteous officer of the Emerald City forces who takes an interest in the unattached young man loitering around the barracks and finds him a place in the service. His good manners survive, undisturbed, the things he orders his soldiers to do.
characters.name: Commander Cherrystone

characters.description: A young officer of the Emerald City forces, good-looking and highly strung, whose duty is the care and training of the government's most closely guarded weapon. He and Liir recognize something in each other, and what he knows about his own work has begun to sicken him.
characters.name: Trism bon Cavalish

recaps.ending: Liir survives the fall that opened the novel, is nursed back to health at the Cloister of Saint Glinda, and finally acts on his own account. He goes to Princess Nastoya, whose spell-held human shape is failing, and helps release her so that she dies as the Elephant she was, among her own people. He puts the birds to work carrying news across a country whose government rules by controlling what people are allowed to know. The identity of that government's head is settled: the Emperor Apostle, who governs Oz as a living saint, is Shell, the dead Witch's brother, the man Liir dealt with in Southstairs. Nor is still not found, though the evidence is that she got out of the prison alive; Trism, separated from Liir after they burned the dragon stables, is likewise unaccounted for. Liir returns to the farm where he left Candle and finds that she has given birth alone and put the baby out of reach of anyone hunting the Witch's line. The child is a girl, and she is green. The book never states outright that Elphaba was Liir's mother, but the daughter settles the question as far as the rest of Oz will care: the line continues, the Emperor of Oz is the child's great-uncle, and everything owed to and against the Witch's name now attaches to an infant. Liir ends the book with a family at last, and hunted for it.
recaps.in_short: About fifteen and nobody's acknowledged son, Liir leaves Kiamo Ko after the Witch's death carrying her cloak and her broom, with one errand: to find Nor, the girl taken from that household by Emerald City soldiers. The search takes him to the Emerald City, down into the prison of Southstairs, where he meets the Witch's brother Shell, and at last into the Emperor's own forces, which carry him south to take part in the destruction of a Quadling village. Drifting afterwards, he investigates a wave of killings in which the dead are found with their faces scraped away, calls a great conference of birds to map them, and traces them to a secret stable of war dragons. With the dragonmaster Trism, who has come to hate his own work, he burns the stables, and is brought down out of the sky in flight. Broken and nameless, he is nursed back by a silent Quadling girl called Candle at a rural cloister. Recovered, he frees the dying Elephant princess Nastoya from the spell holding her in human shape, learns that the Emperor Apostle now ruling Oz is Shell, and comes home to find that Candle has borne and hidden his daughter, a girl with green skin.

recaps.text: Previously, in Wicked: Elphaba Thropp, born green and set apart from everyone around her, grew from a fiercely serious student into a political dissident against the Wizard who ruled Oz and against his persecution of the land's intelligent, speaking Animals. After the death of the Vinkus prince Fiyero, she withdrew to Kiamo Ko, the mountain castle belonging to his family, taking with her a boy named Liir whose origins she never explained to anyone, including him. Living there among Fiyero's widow and children, the household's ancient Nanny and a troop of winged monkeys, she acquired the reputation Oz remembers: the Wicked Witch of the West. Emerald City soldiers eventually carried off the women and children of that household, among them Fiyero's daughter Nor. Elphaba's sister Nessarose, who ruled Munchkinland, was killed by a falling farmhouse, and the girl who had arrived in it, Dorothy, came on to Kiamo Ko and threw water on Elphaba, who died. Left behind were her cloak, her broom, a book of magic, and Liir: a boy of about fifteen who has never been told whether the Witch was his mother, and who has no one to ask.

Maunts travelling through the mountains find a young man lying broken in the road, apparently fallen from a great height, and carry him back to the Cloister of Saint Glinda, a rural convent. He is unconscious, unnamed and not expected to live. The Superior Maunt has him put in the infirmary, where Sister Doctor and Sister Apothecaire disagree about everything concerning him, and sets a newly arrived Quadling girl called Candle to sit with him and play her instrument, on the chance that music will reach what medicine cannot. From here the novel turns back to the years since the Witch's death at Kiamo Ko, when a boy named Liir was left in an emptying castle with the Witch's Nanny, her winged monkeys, her cloak and her broom, and no idea who he was.

Liir leaves Kiamo Ko with Dorothy and her companions and travels east across the Vinkus. On the way the party is taken up by the Scrow, whose princess, Nastoya, is an Elephant trapped by an old spell in human shape; she recognizes Liir's connection to the dead Witch and asks him to come to her when she can no longer hold the disguise, so that she may die as herself. In the Emerald City the Wizard has abandoned the throne, the Scarecrow has been installed on it, and Dorothy departs. Alone and qualified for nothing, Liir sets himself a single task: to find Nor, the girl from the household at Kiamo Ko who was taken away by soldiers years earlier. Her trail leads him down into Southstairs, the enormous prison sunk beneath the city, where he meets Shell, the dead Witch's brother, who trades there in favors and contraband. Liir finds proof that Nor was held in the prison and proof that she got out of it, but he does not find her.

Unable to follow Nor further and with nowhere else to be, Liir drifts into the Emerald City's forces, where a courteous officer named Cherrystone finds him a place. He is fed, uniformed and given a function for the first time in his life, and the service takes him south into Quadling Country on a campaign the men are told is a policing action. What he takes part in there is the destruction of a village and its people, and he comes out of it complicit, unable to argue that he was only following orders. The country he is serving has meanwhile changed shape again: the Scarecrow's reign gives way to an Emperor who governs as a religious figure, styling himself the Emperor Apostle, whose ministry and armies tighten steadily across Oz. Liir leaves the service and keeps moving. In the later thread, at the cloister, the broken man in the infirmary begins to show signs of coming back.

Reports spread of attacks out of the sky in which people and Animals are found dead with their faces scraped away, and no authority in Oz will say what is doing it. Liir, who has the Witch's broom and can fly it after a fashion, sets out to find out for himself. He calls a great assembly of birds, who come in from every quarter of Oz and give him, between them, an account of the country that no government would supply: where the attacks have fallen, and where the things that make them come from. It is the first undertaking Liir manages on his own, and the birds treat him as somebody worth answering.

Following what the birds told him, Liir traces the attacks to their source. The Emperor's forces have been breeding and training dragons in secret, keeping them underground and flying them out at night against the regime's enemies. The officer responsible for them is a young dragonmaster named Trism bon Cavalish, who has come to loathe his own work. The two become lovers, and together they destroy the stables and the dragons in them. It is an act neither of them can be forgiven for, and it puts the whole apparatus of the state on their trail.

Hunted after the destruction of the dragon stables, Liir and Trism are separated in flight, and Liir is brought down out of the sky. The broken man the maunts found in the road is Liir himself, and the two halves of the novel meet. Under Candle's care in the infirmary he slowly returns to himself, and she conceives a child by him in the course of that half-conscious recovery. When soldiers begin taking an interest in the cloister, the Superior Maunt sends the two of them away to a disused farm belonging to the house, where they live quietly and Candle's pregnancy advances. Yackle, the impossibly old woman the maunts keep and ignore, goes on behaving as though Liir's arrival is the event she has spent her whole unaccountable life waiting for.

Liir keeps the promise he made on the road years earlier and goes to Princess Nastoya, whose disguise is failing and who can neither hold her human shape nor shed it. With help, he undoes what is binding her, and she dies as the Elephant she was. He also begins using what he has instead of hiding from it, sending word through the birds so that news travels across Oz faster than the Emperor's ministry can suppress it. The Emperor Apostle, it emerges, is Shell, the dead Witch's brother and the man Liir dealt with in Southstairs, now ruling Oz as a living saint. Liir returns to the farm to find that Candle has given birth alone and hidden the baby to keep her out of the government's reach: a daughter, born with green skin. Nothing in the book confirms outright that Elphaba was Liir's mother, but the child is the strongest evidence anyone has yet had, and she inherits, unasked, everything that goes with the name.

characters.description: The son of Macon and Ruth Dead, born in Michigan after a man's fatal attempt to fly from the roof of a hospital. Growing up in a prosperous but divided Black family, he becomes self-absorbed and restless, conscious that his unusual nickname and a slight physical asymmetry mark him apart.
characters.name: Macon Dead III

characters.description: Milkman's father, a wealthy landlord whose drive to own property grew from childhood loss and insecurity. Severe with his tenants and family, he despises his sister Pilate and wants his son to inherit his hunger for material independence.
characters.name: Macon Dead II

characters.description: Milkman's mother, the refined daughter of the late Dr. Foster. Her marriage is loveless, and she preserves an intense attachment to memories of her father while trying to protect the son whose birth she fought to secure.
characters.name: Ruth Foster Dead

characters.description: Macon's estranged younger sister, a bootlegger who lives without a navel and carries her name in a brass box hanging from one ear. Independent, generous, and rooted in inherited knowledge, she becomes a source of freedom and family history for Milkman.
characters.name: Pilate Dead

characters.description: Milkman's closest friend from boyhood, intelligent and politically alert. His father was killed in racist violence, and his anger at the vulnerability of Black life shapes a worldview very different from Milkman's sheltered detachment.
characters.name: Guitar Bains

characters.description: Pilate's granddaughter and Milkman's cousin. She and Milkman form an intimate attachment when they are young, but they want very different things from the relationship as they grow older.
characters.name: Hagar Dead

characters.description: Pilate's daughter and Hagar's mother, a warm and impulsive woman with an uncanny ability to win prizes. She shares Pilate's unconventional household and deep devotion to Hagar.
characters.name: Reba Dead

characters.description: Milkman's older sister, educated and dutiful, whose abilities have been confined by her father's expectations. She secretly begins a relationship that gives her a life beyond the Dead household.
characters.name: First Corinthians Dead
